Akamai will supply CPUs to Anthropic over seven years in a deal that could reach $20bn. It also issued Anthropic a warrant for about 5% of its common stock, a first for Akamai. Akamai headquarters, 145 Broadway, Cambridge, Massachusetts Anthropic has signed an $11.6bn, seven-year agreement to use Akamai’s cloud infrastructure, Akamai announced after the US market closed on Thursday. The deal can grow by a further $9bn, which would take the total to about $20bn. As part of the deal, Akamai issued Anthropic a warrant for 7.7 million shares on an as-converted basis, about 5% of its common stock. The exercise price is $111.33. The warrant takes the form of non-voting convertible Series B preferred stock. About 2% vests with the $11.6bn commitment. The remaining 3% vests only if the expansion happens, at 1% for every $3bn of extra services. Akamai will supply Anthropic with access to central processing units (CPUs), Bloomberg’s Lynn Doan reported. The contract builds on a $1.8bn deal the two companies signed in May. Akamai shares rose as much as 17% in late trading, to $129.60, according to Bloomberg. “Anthropic is advancing the AI revolution and we are thrilled they chose Akamai’s capabilities for building and operating AI infrastructure at scale,” said Tom Leighton, Akamai’s CEO and co-founder. Akamai expects to spend about $5.5bn in capital to serve the contract. It is raising its 2026 capital spending by about $1.7bn to pre-buy supplies, including memory. The company said the deal does not change its 2026 revenue guidance. According to Bloomberg, the $5.5bn is more than six times what Akamai spent on capital in all of 2025. Leighton told Bloomberg the contract should start in the second half of next year. He expects $150m to $300m in revenue from Anthropic next year, rising to an annual run rate of about $1.7bn by 2028. Leighton also told Bloomberg this is the first time Akamai has agreed to a warrant as part of a cloud deal with a customer. “It’s a serious step, but I think in this case it made sense to do,” Leighton told Bloomberg. “It helps bring the companies together.” Some Wall Street investors have raised concerns about so-called circular AI deals, Bloomberg noted. In those deals, companies that buy each other’s products also invest in one another, which critics say makes real demand for AI harder to measure. The Akamai contract adds to a run of compute agreements by Anthropic this year. It signed a $10bn deal with Volta in August. In September, The Information reported that Anthropic is the customer behind Rum Group’s $13.7bn compute contract. Anthropic also signed its first Australian data centre lease. Bloomberg reported that it has also secured chips from Google and SpaceX. Anthropic was not quoted in Akamai’s announcement. Attackers got into DriveWealth, the US broker behind Revolut's US stock trading, on 4 and 5 September. Revolut says in Europe the DriveWealth breach only involves data from before December 2023. A breach at DriveWealth, the US broker behind Revolut’s US stock trading, exposed the personal data of some Revolut customers. DriveWealth and Revolut emailed affected customers on Thursday. DriveWealth said an unauthorised party got into its network on 4 and 5 September. The access was the result of a social engineering campaign run by unknown third parties, it wrote. The Irish Independent reported on Thursday that the breach reached Revolut customers in Ireland. “This security incident involved unauthorized access to historic personal data we held about you when you directly contracted with us in the past,” DriveWealth wrote. The data may include names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses and employment details, DriveWealth said. It also covers country of citizenship, age, gender and a partial DriveWealth account number. The attackers did not get passwords or payment details such as card or bank account numbers, the broker said. It has reported the incident to the data protection authority in Lithuania. Revolut customers who used its trading service signed two contracts, one with Revolut and one with DriveWealth, Revolut said in its email. Revolut moved EEA customers off that arrangement in December 2023, so the breach can only include data from before then. DriveWealth kept the records to meet its legal and regulatory duties, Revolut said. In the UK and Australia, Revolut made the same change by June 2025, it told the Irish Independent. In the US, the incident covers customers who have used US stock trading. “Your account can’t be accessed solely with the information involved in this incident, and we haven’t detected any unauthorised activity on your account,” Revolut wrote. The breach did not reach Revolut’s own systems, it said, or any Revolut passwords, passcodes, card details or ID documents. Neither company will ask customers for their passcode or tell them to move money to another account, Revolut added. DriveWealth runs US trading for other apps too. Australian broker Stake warned its customers on 21 September. New Zealand’s Hatch followed a day later, 1News reported. For their customers, the exposed data also included portfolio values and cash balances. DriveWealth’s notice on its website lists about 62,000 affected residents of Rhode Island. It says it has found no unauthorised trading, transfers or withdrawals. The DriveWealth breach is the second data incident at Revolut this month. On 12 September, Revolut confirmed it had handed over customer passports to scammers who posed as government officials. The company, valued at $115 billion, is planning a dual stock market listing in London and New York. McDonald’s admits some of its past initiatives hurt its own restaurants. Now it’s spending big to get them back on track. This story has been updated. McDonald’s own menu innovation was hurting the very restaurants it was meant to help. New product launches came so fast that service slowed down and satisfaction dropped, the company admitted at its investor day this week. Now the company is spending $8.5 billion over a ten-year period to fix this issue and more, according to Bloomberg. The investment builds on McDonald’s “Next” growth plan, the company’s broader growth and productivity strategy focused on restaurant modernization, technology deployment, operational simplification and stronger restaurant economics. McDonald’s says the plan should make restaurants run more efficiently enough to add about $100,000 a year in cash flow for the average U.S. location, with most of that money eventually landing in franchisees’ pockets. The company estimates it’ll take about four years for franchisees to earn back what they’re spending Part of the fix involves chasing a market McDonald’s has historically underserved: chicken, a category worth an estimated $30 billion. The company also wants back into the wellness conversation. McDonald’s says 84% of households with a GLP-1 user still visit its restaurants, and it’s building new menu options aimed at that audience. McDonald’s is staking billions on the idea that better-run restaurants, not flashy new products, are what will win back customers. The money would nearly double Amazon Now’s network of small warehouses as it chases Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy. Amazon will spend $3bn to grow its quick-commerce business in India by 2030, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing two people who know the plans directly. Quick commerce is the term for app orders that reach shoppers within minutes. Amazon declined to comment on the figures. It did say, however, that its quick-commerce arm had passed $1bn in annualised gross sales in the last three months. That makes it the fastest-growing part of its Indian e-commerce business so far. According to Reuters, the first $1bn will be spent by the end of 2027 and the other $2bn by 2030. Most of it will pay for new small neighbourhood warehouses for Amazon Now, the service inside the main Amazon app that handles these deliveries. One source told Reuters that Amazon wants about 1,300 of these sites by April, up from roughly 750 today. The rest of the money will go on inventory software, AI tools that predict demand, and a wider range of products. Amazon is starting a long way behind its rivals. Blinkit, Swiggy and Zepto together hold 77% of the market, according to Datum Intelligence data cited by Reuters, while Walmart’s Flipkart has 11% and Amazon has 6.2%. Datum expects the market, worth $19bn today, to reach $41bn by 2030. For now, Amazon plans to stick to everyday essentials. It will not stock products that customers are unlikely to order again, one source said, which is why the service does not sell iPhones as some rivals do. Analysts at Bernstein warned in July that groceries alone cannot pay for the high costs of quick commerce, because orders are small and other goods carry higher margins. Amazon also has to work within India’s strict rules on foreign e-commerce firms. In 2024, the competition regulator found it had favoured some sellers, which Amazon denies. In January, the government also told delivery firms to stop selling their services as 10-minute deliveries, over rider safety concerns. Satish Meena, founder of Datum Intelligence, told Reuters that catching rivals with loyal customers would be hard. Even so, he said Amazon could use offers to move its existing shoppers over to fast delivery.                                        Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. NIQ says 51% of US consumers used an AI shopping tool in the past month, the first time its tracker has passed half. Product recommendations lead, at 20%. Some 51% of US consumers used at least one AI tool to help them shop in the past month, according to new figures from NIQ. It is the first time the share has passed 50% in the market research firm’s Agentic Commerce Tracker. Use has grown steadily over the past two quarters, NIQ said. It now covers every step of a purchase, from finding a product to deciding to buy it. Product recommendations were the most common use, at 20% of consumers. AI personal shopping assistants came next, at 16%. People mostly use AI to compare options, judge value and narrow their choices, the survey found. In NIQ’s words, AI is “compressing decision-making” rather than replacing shopping. “Just months ago, AI-assisted shopping was viewed as an emerging behavior among early adopters. Today, it is now mainstream,” said Liz Buchanan, NIQ’s president for North America. For brands and retailers, that means product content, how easily AI can find a product, and structured product data now matter as much as shelf placement and search rankings, NIQ said. “The path to purchase is rapidly evolving from search-driven to AI-driven, and that change is happening faster than many organizations realize,” Buchanan said. The tracker is a monthly survey. NIQ asks about 500 US consumers each month, as part of its Quick Question research. The tracker also covers Canada, but NIQ published only US figures. NIQ also sells tools to measure this shift. On 2 September, it announced a product with Similarweb that will track how brands show up in ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Perplexity and Claude. It will also measure how much traffic and how many sales come from those AI tools. A first version is due in the fourth quarter of 2026, starting with a few product categories and markets. Similarweb’s own data shows that AI search is fragmenting across several assistants. Payment companies are also working on agents that buy. Visa, Mastercard and Ant International have teamed up on ID checks for agents. Agentic commerce is also changing how people buy their groceries. Wolfsburg is losing the extra shifts that were meant to lift it past 600,000 cars this year, while Emden and Zwickau gain them, ten weeks after both were reported among four German plants facing closure Volkswagen Chattanooga Assembly Plant in Tennessee Volkswagen is now taking more orders for electric cars than for petrol and diesel in Germany, its home market and the largest in Europe, and has cancelled planned extra shifts at Wolfsburg while adding them at Emden and Zwickau. The four budget models driving the shift have taken about 100,000 orders between them and are all built in Spain. Volkswagen is taking more orders for electric cars than for petrol and diesel in Germany, InsideEVs reported, citing Automobilwoche. Germany is its home market and the largest in Europe. The company is now rewriting production schedules across several plants. Wolfsburg builds the petrol cars. The historic plant makes the Golf, Tiguan and Tayron, and Volkswagen had planned additional shifts to lift this year’s output from 580,000 vehicles to more than 600,000. Those shifts have been cancelled. Demand for combustion models has fallen away. Two other plants gain. Emden, which assembles the ID.7, is getting at least two special shifts, and Zwickau, which builds the updated ID.3 Neo, is raising output. In July both were among four German sites reported as candidates for closure, alongside Hanover and Audi’s Neckarsulm. Volkswagen confirmed none of that on the record. The cars selling best are Spanish. The ID Polo has taken more than 40,000 orders, and the Cupra Raval, Skoda Epiq and Volkswagen ID Cross have added roughly 60,000 between them. All four make up the Electric Urban Car Family, and all four are built in Spain rather than Germany. Volkswagen put the money there. More than EUR 3B went into transforming the Martorell plant and about EUR 10B into electrifying its Spanish operations. The four cars share one platform, which the company says saved EUR 600M and cut production complexity. The ID Polo is expected to start at around EUR 25,000. Size is a policy question now. At 4.05 metres the ID Polo sits under the 4.2 metre cap the European Commission proposed for a small-car category, whose members would get favourable treatment in fleet carbon calculations if built in the union. Audi’s own A2 e-tron, made in Ingolstadt, misses that cap by 12 centimetres. The margins are the catch. Volkswagen makes less money on an electric car than on a comparable combustion one, so a demand shift it did not expect arrives in the middle of a restructuring in which up to 100,000 job cuts have been reported and never confirmed. The plants gaining shifts this month are two of the four that were being discussed for closure ten weeks ago. The new Beats 360 headphones are available for purchase at many Apple Stores around the world as of today. Retailers like Best Buy and Target also have some stock available in stores. Apple's Beats brand announced the headphones earlier this week after teasing them for several months. The Beats 360 are over-ear headphones with a design similar to the AirPods Max and interchangeable ear cushions so you can swap colors. Compared with the Beats Studio Pro, the Beats 360 have up to 1.75x more noise cancellation and improved sound quality. Features like Personalized Spatial Audio, Transparency mode, and Adaptive EQ are supported, as are fast pairing and automatic device switching. They have IPX4 sweat and water resistance, making them suitable for the gym. The Beats 360 work with two kinds of cushions. The Performance Knit memory foam cushions are breathable and meant for working out, while the UltraPlush cushions have a softer, more pillowy feel. The Beats 360 ship with the Performance Knit cushions, and the UltraPlush can be purchased separately. Beats 360 are priced at $349.99, and for a limited time, Apple is selling add-on ear cushions for a discounted $9.99 price through October 31. Headphone colors include Black, Cloud, Pink, and Sky. By          Stephan Bisaha                        A for sale sign sits in front of a home in Miami.                                                           Joe Raedle/Getty Images                                       hide caption  The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage leaped to 7.03% on Thursday, according to the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., which also goes by Freddie Mac. This is the first time the rate has passed the 7% mark in 20 months, or since January 2025. While the 7% mortgage rate milestone holds no literal significance beyond the psychological effect of the round number, the sharp rise in rates since March risks further squeezing the budgets of homebuyers. And it's bound to deepen the freeze on a housing market held stagnant for years by the high cost of homeownership. Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year Treasury note, which has risen sharply over the summer amid concerns about high inflation as well as the size of the federal debt. The Federal Reserve last week raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point — its first move this year — and many policymakers projected it may raise it one more time before year's end. Investors are bracing for potentially even more rate hikes to help fight inflation. High mortgage rates contributed to a 2% decline in existing home sales in August from the previous month, according to the National Association of Realtors. The median sale for an existing home was about $429,000. At that price, a single percentage point increase in the mortgage rate can cost buyers hundreds of additional dollars a month and tens of thousands over the life of the loan. Housing researchers had hoped 2026 would provide a break for buyers and sellers waiting for cheaper rates and those savings. For a brief moment, that seemed to happen as mortgage rates fell below 6% by the end of February. But they quickly shot back up with the war with Iran, which has led to volatility in the bond markets. Continued fighting has also prolonged worries about inflation, further helping push up mortgage rates. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. September 24, 2026 12:00pm by 			        Barry Ritholtz    Last month, I posted this data dive into the question of “How Wealth Is Created in America.” It’s always fun to look at the sources of wealth, and I used a few broad data sources.1 But these create a very blunt, 10,000-foot view of wealth in America. It would be great if there was a more granular look at where wealth came from – its sources, who is rich, and where they live nationwide. Just imagine how thrilled I was a few weeks later to see Owen Zidar and Eric Zwicks’ new book “The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There.” I had them on At the Money yesterday,2 discussing the book generally (podcast here; transcript here). Part Two will be out next week and will focus on all the insane data on wealth in the book. One data point worth discussing was also the biggest surprise I found in their book: the impact of no-competes: The $300 Billion Noncompete Penalty: Over 20% of American workers are subject to noncompete agreements, which restrict employees from switching to local competitors or starting their own firms. Banning noncompete agreements nationwide would boost comp by $300B annually. $300 billion annually is a giant shift of cash from Labor to Capital, but my assumption was this was a necessary evil to protect work product and IP; think of senior people at tech firms with intimate knowledge of patents and processes – even the secret formula for Coca-Cola.3 What surprised me was the aggressive use of non-competes for jobs like “Sandwich Artists” at hoagie places such as Jimmy John’s and Jersey Mike’s. Slapping some meat, cheese, greens, and condiments onto slices of bread is not what non-competes were created for. That is a very anti-competitive, anti-free-market way to keep wages artificially suppressed. “Sandwich Artist” may be a laughable job title, but the attorneys behind this deserve some credit for “Bullshit Artists” of the highest caliber… More next week…       Previously: How Wealth Is Created in America (August 19, 2026) At The Money: Who Is Wealthy in America (and How Did They Get Rich?) The International Federation of Robotics counted a record 603,000 new industrial robots in 2025, and 59% went to China. The US overtook Japan, while EU installations fell 11%. Factories around the world installed 603,000 industrial robots in 2025, up 11%, and China accounted for 354,000 of them, or 59%. The figures come from the International Federation of Robotics (IFR), which published its World Robotics 2026 report on Thursday. The number of robots at work in factories rose 9% to a record 5 million, more than double the figure seven years ago, the IFR said. The federation is a non-profit that represents more than 3,000 organisations, including robot makers. Its president, Jane Heffner, is also a global vice president at Teradyne Robotics. “The strongest growth is taking place in Asia, followed by Americas. Europe is moving ahead more slowly,” Heffner said. China’s installations grew 20% in 2025, beating its previous record by almost 60,000 units. Chinese brands sold 195,000 of those robots, up 15%. That gave them 55% of their home market, down from 57% in 2024, as foreign suppliers grew faster, by 27%. Electronics makers were the biggest buyers, with 96,400 units. Car makers installed a record 78,900, up 38%, and the metal and machinery industry 78,700, up 44%. Not every new market held up. Food and beverage installations fell 37% after rising 86% in 2024, and textiles dropped by 92%. “China’s success in modernising its industrial system is based on its national robotics strategy, which was initiated ten years ago,” Heffner said. The latest update of that strategy is part of the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026 to 2030. It points China’s AI research at physical uses, with robots as the main drivers of growth, Heffner said in the IFR’s China report. The federation expects the Chinese market to grow by 5% to 10% a year until 2029, because an ageing population is leaving factories short of workers. The United States installed 38,400 robots, up 12%, and overtook Japan as the second-largest market. It was the third-strongest year on record for the US, behind 2018 and 2022, the IFR said in its US report. “Growth came from the food industry and sectors like warehousing, logistics or medical. At the same time automotive has stayed stable as the largest customer,” Heffner said. Car makers installed 13,500 robots in the US, down 1%, and food and beverage companies 2,900, up 30%. Most robots in the US are still imported from Japan and Europe, according to the IFR. Japan installed 36,219 units, down 19% and its lowest total in a decade. South Korea stayed fourth with about 30,000, down 1%. India rose to sixth place with almost 10,500, up 15%. The EU installed 60,500 robots in 2025, down 11%, the IFR said in its EU report. Asia installed 457,315, up 14%, and the Americas 57,044, also up 14%. The number of robots working in EU factories still passed 700,000 for the first time. At 712,000, it is more than 80% higher than in 2015. Germany remains the largest market in Europe and the fifth-largest in the world. It installed 24,842 robots, 41% of the EU total, but 8% fewer than in 2024. The IFR noted that Germany remains in recession. Italy installed 7,800, down 11%, France 4,500, down 8%, and Spain 4,300, down 15%. Across the EU, car makers cut their installations by 25% to 14,900. Chinese suppliers are also moving into the EU, and the first have set up European distribution hubs, the IFR said. Trade restrictions in other key markets such as the US might speed that up. European companies are building their own hardware too, such as the robot compute modules planned by NEURA and SECO. The IFR expects global installations to rise 9% to 655,000 in 2026 and reach 806,000 in 2029. It forecasts 11% growth in Asia this year, 2% in the Americas and none in Europe. From 2027 to 2029, it expects Europe to grow by 6% a year, ahead of the Americas at 2% but behind Asia at 8%. Humanoid robots remain a small part of the market. Nearly 7,000 full-size humanoids, taller than 140cm, were sold worldwide in 2025, according to the IFR. It counts 174 humanoid makers, more than half of them in China, and many were founded only recently, like the Japanese startup O-ID, which is building modular humanoid robots. China’s data regulator plans standards for embodied AI data, and Beijing is reportedly slowing humanoid robot IPOs. The IFR said humanoids are still making the leap from laboratories to pilots. Safety, reliability, a lack of training data and the lack of a viable business case all stand in the way, it said. The pitch never changes. Buy the robot, reclaim your weekends, and let the floors clean themselves while you do anything else. I bought in. Then I bought in again a week later, adding a second eufy X10 Pro Omni for the basement after the first one won me over upstairs. Months of daily runs later, here's the part the ad copy skips: these didn't hand me my time back. They rearranged my chores and slapped new labels on them. Some of that trade was worth it. Plenty of it started with an afternoon and a $30 rubber ramp just to coax the robot over a single doorway. That is not the effortless helper the box promised. The robot doesn't work the moment you unbox it. Mine needed mapping passes to learn the floor plan, then boundary lines drawn in the app so it would quit trying to eat the same rug fringe. Then came the invisible daily tax: a lap around each room to clear cords, chargers, stray socks, and shoelaces before every run, because a $700 machine will happily wind a charging cable around its brush roll and drag it across the house. The doorway problem was its own project. My basement had a floor transition tall enough that the robot treated it like a wall, bouncing off and looping back every single time. Fixing it meant researching, buying, and cutting down a rubber ramp to fit the frame. None of this is hard. But hard was never the promise. Effortless was, and effortless doesn't include a pre-clean tidy-up or a weekend spent solving a threshold the robot couldn't climb. A premium robot vacuum that delivers on its promises.  A robot vacuum running while you're home isn't a time-saver. It's a moving obstacle. It bumps a chair leg, pauses at your feet, and turns a quiet morning into a slow game of dodge-the-robot. The real value shows up only when it runs while the house is empty, which means the hands-off appliance depends entirely on you nailing the timing. Left to a basic daily schedule, mine used to fire up mid-morning while someone was always around to work around it. My fix was to stop scheduling by the clock and start scheduling by event. I tied the eufy to a door sensor so it only kicks off after the last person leaves, using an Alexa routine built on a cheap contact sensor. That solved it. It also proves the point. The one effortless version of this appliance was something I had to build, not something I bought. The all-in-one dock is the feature that sells these premium models, and it's great, right up until it becomes another item on your list. The X10 Pro Omni empties its own bin, washes its own mop pads, and refills its own water. What it doesn't do is manage the consumables that make all of that possible. I still swap the dust bag when it fills. I still dump the dirty-water tank and top off the clean one, because the mop can't wash floors with sludge. Hair wraps around the brush roll and the side spinner no matter what the anti-tangle marketing claims, so I'm on the floor with scissors every couple of weeks. The self-cleaning station cleans itself less than the name suggests. Add it up, and the maintenance-free robot needs maybe 10 minutes of hands-on attention a week. That's far less than vacuuming by hand. It's not zero, and the marketing sold me zero.  Here's the scenario the ads never show. A glass tips over, or a snack ends up across the kitchen floor, and the last thing that makes sense is opening an app to summon a robot that trundles over three minutes later and smears the mess into a wider circle. For anything urgent, I reach for the cordless. My aging Dyson V8, that I kept alive with a $22 battery adapter, still handles spills, stairs, and upholstery faster than any robot on a timer. That's the honest division of labor in my house. The robot keeps the open floors at a steady baseline so dust and crumbs never pile up. The stick vacuum does the reactive work, the messes that won't wait for a scheduled 9 a.m. run. One maintains. The other actually cleans.  I'm not returning either eufy. For keeping hardwood and tile at a hands-off baseline, they earn their spot, and the door-sensor trick means I rarely think about the upstairs floors at all. The disappointment was never the hardware. It was the story sold around it. A robot vacuum is a floor-maintenance tool, not a time machine, and once you treat it that way, the resentment fades. Set that expectation going in, pair it with a couple of smart routines, and you'll get real value. If you want the effortless part to actually feel effortless, that's worth building into your wider home automation. We want to hear from you. A series exploring the companies, leaders, and workers who are at the forefront of the AI supply-chain revolution. Fall has just begun, but for companies in the Halloween candy and costume business, spooky season kicked off this summer. At Mars — the maker of candies like M&Ms, Twix, and Skittles — they've found that consumers want to maximize their Halloween festivities, Ramesh Kollepara, the SVP and global chief technology officer of the company's snacking division, told Business Insider. They're leaning into "Summerween" by buying trick-or-treat candy in July, Kollepara said, pointing to Mars' recent in-house report on consumer candy trends. "That means we have to think beyond a traditional Halloween selling window," Kollepara said. "We need to understand not only how much demand we'll see, but when it will begin, where it will occur, and how the product mix may change." For this reason, Kollepara called Halloween "a great stress test" for supply chains. There's added complexity because the Halloween shopping season has a fixed deadline for merchandise to reach stores, said Benjamin Bond, SVP of client strategy and success at Simbe, a retail robotics and AI company. At the same time, ordering too much stock leads to waste. For manufacturers like Mars and retailers like Walmart, AI helps find the sweet spot. Previously, supply chain planners manually adjusted parameters, and forecasts were trial and error, said Madhav Durbha, the group VP of manufacturing industry strategy at AI platform RELEX Solutions. Now AI automates changes, so planners aren't "constantly fiddling with the algorithms," he said. Mars has turned to AI to track and plan when its treats are in high demand. AI layers in data showing consumers are buying earlier, as well as Mars' available inventory, production capacity, and customer requirements, Kollepara said. At Mars, AI connects the dots among four key questions, with results that can vary by geographic region and consumer behavior, Kollepara said. Those questions are: For instance, Mars' research found that consumers in the Western US want Halloween-themed novelty treats, while those in the South prefer gummy candy, allowing Mars to route its inventory accordingly. Like Mars, Walmart's use of AI in the supply chain begins with forecasting, Indira Uppuluri, the retailer's SVP of supply chain technology, told Business Insider. Walmart pulls last year's Halloween data, new candy releases, and social media trends, then analyzes the data using AI to inform the orders it places with suppliers, Uppuluri said. Walmart monitors its distribution networks with AI to ensure products are packed and transported in time for trick-or-treaters. Its AI reviews what's in each trailer and compares it with the current store inventory. The system then flags which trailers to unload right away, and which can wait — a useful tool during the holiday rush. "At the end of the day, it's the flow that's super important for us," Uppuluri said. "There's always something coming in; there's always something going out. How do we get the right movement for the right inventory?" Getting products to warehouses is only part of the Halloween supply chain puzzle, Bond said. Retailers must also move inventory from stores' backrooms to shelves and respond to shifts in demand at speed. "Stores have roughly a 10-day window around peak demand to get the season right," Bond said. During the season, if Walmart's AI recognizes signs of too much or too little inventory, "we course correct along the way," Uppuluri said. It might tell a vendor to pause on sending an order if there's too much unsold candy. As candy and costumes arrive at Walmart's distribution centers, automation technology sorts the goods into pallets based on where the merchandise will go in store aisles, Uppuluri said. That way, store associates can quickly unload goods and stock shelves. Walmart builds seasonal merchandise pallets early and holds them at distribution centers to avoid crowding store backrooms, which have more limited space than warehouses. When a store needs inventory, a pallet is ready to go. The pallets also have IoT tags and RFID tags, so Walmart can ensure they're dropped off at the right store. For all the complex algorithms running in the background, the indicator of success is simple: whether a consumer can get the candy and costumes they want, Uppuluri said. He added: "You can have smart systems, but if you don't make that assortment available to customers when they need it, nothing else matters." No comments right now, check back later. The AG says the prediction market is operating in New York without a license. New York Attorney General Letitia James on Thursday filed suit against the prediction market Polymarket, accusing it of being an illegal gambling operation that is operating in New York without a license. The lawsuit mirrors the one James' office filed against the prediction market Kalshi and, if successful, could affect Polymarket's ability to operate. The suit asks a court to order Polymarket to forfeit money, distribute restitution, and pay fines. Polymarket launched in the United States in December 2025 as a service that allowed users to bet money on the outcome of sporting events, and has expanded to allow wagers on everything from current events to weather patterns. As the world's largest prediction market platform, the service, according to one estimate, is on pace to facilitate more than $70 billion in trading in 2026 -- more than triple the volume it handled in 2025.  Polymarket's global website, registered in Panama, is supposed to be off limits in the U.S., and the U.S.-approved version of the site offers fewer trades than its international platform. But there is evidence that many Americans have managed to access the international site -- which offers trading on subjects like war, which is banned in the U.S. -- using digital workarounds, like virtual private networks known as VPNs.  James suit claims that Polymarket's prediction market is an illegal, unlicensed gambling operation that exposes New Yorkers -- including those under the legal gambling age of 21 -- to serious personal and financial risk. State law prohibits wagering on games involving New York college teams and all sports betting for those under 21. "Our gambling laws exist to protect New Yorkers, prevent the potential harms of problem gambling, and ensure funding for educational and public benefit programs," James said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.   Polymarket's chief legal officer said in a statement that the platform would fight the suit. "Polymarket was founded in a tiny NYC apartment and now has more than 350 employees here, embodying why people and businesses come here to make it. We believe in New York and we're staying here," said chief legal officer Neal Kumar. "While the AG's decision to copy/paste a recycled lawsuit is disappointing, we'll fight for our users." "Any time the AG's office wants to swing by, our door is open for a conversation about how we protect consumers and offer fair, transparent and legal markets," the statement said. The platform has insisted its event contracts are federally regulated derivatives outside the scope of state gaming laws. James' lawsuit, however, said Polymarket's prediction markets meet the legal definition of gambling because the outcomes of the events on which its users are betting are uncertain and outside the control of the bettor, or hinge on a game of chance. Despite this, the lawsuit said, Polymarket has failed to obtain a license from the New York State Gaming Commission, allegedly sidestepping its obligation to pay taxes like licensed casinos and mobile sports gambling platforms do. Multiple lawsuits across the country claim prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi fall under state jurisdiction -- but if James' suit is successful, Polymarket could be forced to pay billions of dollars and change the way it operates nationwide. "By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement at the time of the filing of the suit. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

Tech > Mobile > Phones With freshly unveiled Snapdragon 8 Elite chips, Xiaomi's 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max represent a new generation of Android flagship devices. Principal Writer Principal Writer September 23, 2026, 11:55 pm ET Chinese tech giant Xiaomi is officially the first phone-maker to use Qualcomm’s freshly unveiled premium chipsets in its new flagship phones. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max were announced on Wednesday in Beijing and are powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, respectively, making them two of the most powerful smartphones on the market right now. But that market is initially limited to China, although a global launch for the phones will take place before the end of 2026. Like other Xiaomi phones, they won’t be coming to the US. I went hands-on with the phones at the Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, where Qualcomm had lifted the lid on the new chips just 24 hours earlier. The two models look almost identical aside from size and bear more than a passing resemblance to the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which are also new this month. More from CNET One major difference is the rear OLED screen, which sits beside the camera module (and was also on the 17 Pro series). Xiaomi says this display can show important notifications when your phone is face down on the table — a little like Nothing’s light-up glyph system — allowing you to mindfully disengage from scrolling without completely cutting yourself off. For this particular use case, I think Nothing might have the edge, as less time looking at screens is probably better for us. But I enjoyed the widgets and animated wallpapers, as well as the upgraded selfie-shooting experience the display unlocks. Even though front-facing cameras have improved dramatically in recent years, photo quality can never quite compare with the pictures rear cameras deliver. But the second screen lets you use the rear camera for selfies and vlogging, just as you might use the front camera on your phone. I’m a longtime fan of Xiaomi’s cameras, and while I haven’t had a chance to fully test the 18 Pro Max, the company’s previous phones and continued partnership with Leica give me every reason to hope this new generation will continue to deliver. The 18 Pro Max has a 200-megapixel main camera, a 200-megapixel telephoto camera that supports macro photography as close as 12 centimeters (4.72 inches), and a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera. In my brief hands-on time with the phone, I was pleased with the quality of the selfies I snapped — they’d have been straight to Instagram if it had been my own phone. Another standout feature of the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max is the Privacy Display, which works similarly to Samsung’s technology of the same name on the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Privacy Display restricts viewing angles so you can see only the screen when you’re looking at it straight on. With Xiaomi’s version, you can choose whether to apply the tech to the full screen, individual apps or split screen, so that it blocks only the top or bottom. I tried this out with Privacy Display applied to the gallery at the top half of the screen. I could still make out the general shapes on the display, but it did obscure and darken the details, so I couldn’t see the content of the photos when I turned the phone to the side. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max that I saw were both China editions featuring 7,000-mAh and 8,500-mAh silicon-carbon batteries, respectively. The versions that eventually go on sale in Europe and other regions may have different specs, but we won’t have long to wait to find out, with the global launch coming within the next few months. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Entrepreneurs love the idea of diversification. After building one successful company, the temptation is to chase the next opportunity that comes along. A friend pitches a restaurant concept. Someone mentions a real estate deal. A franchise becomes available. Before long, the entrepreneur owns several businesses in completely unrelated industries. It looks like growth. More often, it’s fragmentation. Over the years, I’ve learned that expansion works best when each new business strengthens the others. Instead of building a collection of unrelated companies, we focused on building an ecosystem. Every new venture had to support the businesses we already owned while creating more value for customers, employees and stakeholders. That approach helped us build companies across physical therapy, healthcare staffing, hospice care, consulting and technology. More importantly, it allowed each business to generate opportunities for the others instead of competing for our time and attention. Many entrepreneurs believe diversification reduces risk. In my experience, random diversification increases complexity and weakens focus. Strategic ecosystems do the opposite. They improve efficiency, strengthen margins and create momentum that compounds over time. Several years ago, I noticed a pattern among business owners who came to me for advice about expansion. Many were chasing opportunities simply because they looked profitable. One entrepreneur owned a successful service company and wanted to buy a restaurant. Another ran a thriving healthcare practice and was exploring a retail concept. Neither opportunity had any connection to the existing business. When I asked how the new venture would support their current operation, the answer was usually the same: “It won’t. I just think it could make money.” Revenue alone doesn’t make something strategic. A new business should strengthen your existing platform. It should create operational advantages, shared resources, stronger customer relationships or new market opportunities. If it does none of those things, you’re adding complexity without creating leverage. Our ecosystem grew as we identified related needs within the same market. It started with physical therapy. As our practice grew, healthcare organizations kept contacting us looking for qualified therapists. At the same time, therapists were reaching out looking for work. That gap led us to launch our company. Rather than starting a completely separate company, we built an extension of what we already understood. The staffing business deepened our industry relationships, expanded our reach and created value across the organization. More recently, technology has become another extension of that ecosystem. Our digital tools and automation support multiple business units instead of serving a single company. Each addition strengthened the whole system. Ecosystems work in part because they reduce dependence on outside providers. Many entrepreneurs focus only on increasing revenue. Fewer focus on controlling the critical parts of their value chain. When a healthcare company relies entirely on outside staffing agencies, for example, it pays a premium every time it needs talent. When staffing becomes part of the ecosystem, those resources can be coordinated more efficiently, and the organization gains another revenue stream The same principle applies in almost every industry. A manufacturer can add distribution. A software company can launch implementation services. A consulting firm can create training programs. Each move captures more value while improving control over quality and execution. Before pursuing any new opportunity, I encourage entrepreneurs to ask four questions. 1. Does this business serve the same customer?Expansion is easier when customers already trust your brand. If the new venture solves another problem for the same audience, you gain efficiency in marketing, sales and relationship building. 2. Does it strengthen an existing capability?The best opportunities build on strengths you already have. Your expertise, infrastructure, talent or relationships should give you an advantage from day one. 3. Will it create opportunities for your other businesses?Every new venture should generate value beyond its own revenue. Look for ways it can create referrals, operational support or strategic advantages for the broader organization. 4. Can it run without draining your attention?Many ideas look attractive until they start consuming leadership bandwidth. If an opportunity requires an entirely new skill set, industry knowledge base or management structure, it may create more distraction than value. A simple framework for planning your ecosystem Entrepreneurs often overcomplicate expansion decisions. I prefer a straightforward approach. Start with your core business and identify the main problem you solve. Next, map the challenges your customers face before, during and after they work with you. Then ask where additional services, products or capabilities could improve their outcomes. Finally, prioritize the opportunities that create shared resources, operational efficiencies or stronger customer relationships. The goal is a connected system that delivers more value with each addition. The biggest lesson I’ve learned about expansion is that success comes from building the right businesses, not more of them. Random diversification creates the appearance of growth while quietly draining focus and energy. Ecosystem thinking creates alignment. Every company strengthens the others. OpenAI saw disappointing results working with Apple to integrate ChatGPT in Siri, according to court documents filed [PDF] in its ongoing legal fight with Elon Musk's company SpaceXAI (xAI at the time the lawsuit was filed). Apple added ChatGPT to ‌Siri‌ in December 2024, but users had to go through a multistep opt-in process, which added a layer of friction. By January 2025, OpenAI said the integration was "off to a slow start" and the company cut its forecast for the number of incremental logged-in weekly active users that it expected to get from the partnership. Much of the filing is redacted, but OpenAI said that by the time Musk's companies filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple and OpenAI, "it was clear that Apple's integration of ChatGPT was dramatically underperforming." In a later section of the filing, OpenAI said again that the Apple integration was "persistently underperforming," leading to a March 2026 conversation between Apple and OpenAI that is redacted. OpenAI asked Apple for a two-year exclusivity period, but Apple refused. The agreement between the two companies explicitly said the deal was non-exclusive and Apple had the right to "integrate products or services that provide the same or similar functionality as [ChatGPT]." Apple told OpenAI that it planned to integrate one provider and then add more, and it made similar statements publicly when announcing the feature. Apple also signed a deal with Google, and Apple's newest models are based on Gemini. OpenAI's filing disputes many of the claims in the xAI lawsuit. Musk alleged OpenAI and Apple had an exclusive deal and that the agreement harmed xAI's growth and customer acquisition. OpenAI says the contract proves there was no exclusive deal, and even if there were, xAI can't prove harm because the ChatGPT ‌Siri‌ integration just didn't draw many new ChatGPT users.  Even if the Court assumes that Apple users who elect to use ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence are foreclosed from OpenAI's rivals (which they are not), the amount of foreclosure caused by the Agreement is indisputably de minimis. While Plaintiffs' experts declined to calculate foreclosure shares, OpenAI's expert, Dr. Catherine Tucker, calculated the share of GenAI consumers who accessed ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence across multiple metrics using the same data and market definition relied upon by Plaintiffs' experts. On these assumptions, Dr. Tucker found foreclosure shares of [REDACTED] across all metrics, consistent with OpenAI's internal view that Apple Intelligence saw minimal usage. Musk's companies dropped their claims against Apple earlier this month, leaving OpenAI as the sole defendant in the lawsuit. Tech > Computing > Gadgets > Photography > Cameras It’s not all about the latest camera gear – the astronauts relied on both old and new tech that anyone can buy off-the-shelf. Senior Writer Senior Writer September 24, 2026, 7:00 am ET Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen takes photos of the moon through a window shroud using a Nikon camera. The picture of him was captured using an iPhone 17 Pro Max. When NASA’s Artemis II mission put humans at the far side of the moon for the first time in 44 years, it often felt like we were there in the capsule with astronauts Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen and Reid Wiseman. That’s almost entirely due to the frequent transmission of imagery from the flight, from live feeds to high-resolution photos that let us look at the moon and life in space like never before. But getting those photos and videos isn’t as easy as tossing a camera in a bag for an Earth-bound vacation. To capture the high-resolution images that made us gasp here on the ground, the astronauts shot with Nikon DSLR and mirrorless cameras. Artemis II used GoPro Hero4 cameras for interior and exterior video feeds, and the crew took many notable photos inside the capsule using iPhone 17 Pro Max phones. As NASA moves toward the Artemis III mission in 2027 and an expected moon landing in 2028 there will undoubtedly be a huge demand to document and share everything that goes on. To get a better understanding of what’s involved with making sure astronauts can capture those historical and candid moments, I spoke to Michael Corrado, Nikon senior manager of Pro Services. “Just to see these pictures come back from space, we couldn’t be more humbled as a company,” Corrado said. “And as an individual, my dad was part of the space program… so it’s in the legacy here.” Corrado also walked me through the rigorous process NASA requires to certify equipment for space travel, why astronauts primarily rely on decade-old tech and how future flights will look different. It also struck me that even these Nikon professionals, who have worked with NASA astronauts and teams for decades, were still gobsmacked by the imagery that comes back. “We were just sitting there in awe of what we were seeing every day,” Corrado said. The Artemis II vehicle – the Orion spacecraft and Integrity capsule – represented some of the latest space flight technology, but not all of the cameras were cutting-edge. For video, NASA used several GoPro Hero4 cameras mounted inside and outside the Artemis II spacecraft, a compact action camera model that came out in 2014. The workhorse of the mission was the Nikon D5 DSLR, a model first introduced to the consumer market in 2016. Also on the flight was the half-decade-old Nikon Z9 mirrorless camera body, introduced in 2021. A photographer here on Earth might pass over the Nikon D5 as an outdated camera, but Corrado suggests that NASA doesn’t view it as “old technology.” “I’d use the word ‘trusted’ technology more than anything,” quipped Corrado. Artemis II commander, Reid Wiseman and Canadian Space Agency mission specialist, Jeremy Hansen (background), training in a mockup of the Orion capsule at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in July 2025. Nikon’s cameras are the only ones fully certified to fly on NASA missions, a spot on the equipment roster the company has maintained since the later Apollo missions in the 1970s. Of the Artemis II lineup, only the Nikon D5 carries the certification badge; the Nikon Z9 is still being evaluated – in that case under real-world conditions. Certification is as much about safety as it is about performance. Camera batteries can be flammable, and flame is the last thing you want in a space capsule. But the camera’s electronics also need to be shielded against radiation. We enjoy a buffer from Earth’s atmosphere, but radiation in open space is another matter. So, although the cameras on the mission are mostly stock models, they’ve been reinforced with internal shielding. “Back in the day, we used to strip things off the camera [like] the leather,” Corrado said, referring to the missions in the 1970s. “They were almost naked cameras that went up. But none of that has to happen with the D5 and the Z9.” There also wasn’t a lot of equipment. When I go out to shoot a sunrise, I’ll typically bring a backup camera in case something goes wrong with my main body. Traveling 250,000 miles from the nearest camera store, I’d expect there to be backups, but since weight is such an issue during spaceflight, Corrado noted that no backup bodies accompanied the astronauts on Artemis II. Today’s cameras are advanced enough that their automatic modes can cover almost any photo situation, and if a shot isn’t quite right we can edit it easily in software. In a dark scene, for example, a camera will increase the ISO to compensate and introduce digital noise, which can then be cleaned up in Lightroom. The photos that came back from the Artemis II mission, though, revealed that the astronauts never leaned on that type of automatic crutch. The dark shots – it’s space, after all – sometimes had high ISOs but not to the point of introducing excessive noise. In an extremely harsh lighting environment, they knew how to take advantage of the wide dynamic range of the D5 and Z9 cameras to avoid moon surfaces blown out too white to preserve surface details. Photos from the dark side of the moon, the first captured in 55 years, reveal formations that scientists will be studying for years. One of my favorite images is a shot of the back of the moon with the Earth rising behind it. You can see details of clouds and the peaks of continents on the illuminated portion of the planet, versus a sliver of bright white like you’d get when taking a snapshot of the moon from your backyard. Keep in mind that the images NASA published during the mission are the ones captured in-camera, not edited raw images, again demonstrating the astronauts’ photographic skills. After years of service, the Nikon D5 is likely looking at NASA retirement. “We worked for years to get the D5 certified for use in space,” Corrado said, “and now it has probably seen its last launch.” The Z9 is taking over for the future, which means it’s currently going through the official certification process even though it’s been around the moon. In fact, Artemis wasn’t the first time the Z9 has gone to space. Astronaut Don Pettit used it for about eight months on the International Space Station. Corrado said there are currently 20 Nikon Z9 cameras on the ISS. “Life is different when you wake up to an email that you think is spam that says ‘Greetings from orbit’,” said Corrado. Pettit’s real-(off)-world experience and questions made their way to Nikon’s engineers. He noted that the feedback typically results in firmware changes specific for NASA. The hardened Z9 that will reach the lunar surface in 2028 will be wrapped in a thermal blanket as part of a system called the Handheld Universal Lunar Camera (HULC). The cover will protect the camera from the moon’s extreme temperature fluctuations. It’s not fair to see the visual riches of the existing Artemis II photos and still have a wishlist, but I think depth is one element missing. Wiseman talked about witnessing land formations on the moon’s surface, saying, “It’s just everything from the training but in three dimensions and absolutely unbelievable.” That makes me wish the crew had captured footage using the Spatial Video feature on their iPhones (I’ve found no evidence that they did). Imagine putting on an Apple Vision Pro and seeing the moon in an immersive way that’s even closer to what the astronauts experienced. Stereoscopic footage could be recorded in the future, though. Nikon is working on a depth camera, for which it was granted a patent in 2025. “We’re still working with NASA very closely… together on these technologies,” Corrado said. No matter what form the future images from Artemis III and future Artemis flights take, they’re sure to be stunning thanks to the astronauts’ training and the crews at Nikon and NASA working to equip them with the hardened camera equipment the missions require.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. High standards do more than help you win, because they keep the wrong people, projects and habits from quietly draining your company’s time, focus and profits. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Many leaders see high standards purely as a tool for achievement, whether that means gaining a competitive edge or outperforming the market. For years, I saw them that way too, judging my organizations mostly by execution and output. But working in multiple executive roles has taught me something deeper: High standards are fundamentally a form of protection. They shield a leader’s career, team and company from the slow, compounding damage of mediocrity. When you set high standards, low-quality inputs, whether in hiring, partnerships or daily habits, get filtered out before they can cause problems. Over several years, that protection is worth far more to a business than any single quarterly win. High standards aren’t about demanding perfection. They’re about building a strong filter that protects the health of the whole organization. To run a complex organization well, treat your standards as a filter everything must pass through. Every partnership you pursue, investment you make, client you take on and behavior you tolerate should meet them. When standards are loose or low, the filter breaks down. Misaligned goals, unhealthy team dynamics and unnecessary complexity start to spread through the culture. The result is a business weighed down by obligations it shouldn’t have taken on, constant internal friction and decisions it comes to regret. Strong standards change how an organization spends its energy. People who don’t meet your professional or behavioral bar don’t get hired. Opportunities that don’t fit get declined. Situations that slow the company down get addressed. This isn’t about arrogance. It’s about protecting your team’s time and focus. By keeping the noise out, leaders create room for focused, intentional work instead of constant firefighting. McLaren Racing offers a clear example of standards coming first. When Zak Brown joined the team in 2016, McLaren had drifted far from its championship history. Results on the track were poor, performance benchmarks had slipped and the team’s culture was fragmented. Brown did make changes at the top, bringing in new drivers and eventually replacing a handful of senior leaders. But the rest of the team, roughly a thousand people, stayed the same. What changed was how they worked together. McLaren set clear expectations for how engineering teams communicated across departments, how problems were raised and solved without finger-pointing and which lapses were no longer acceptable. Those standards were designed to protect the team from the habits that had held it back: blame-shifting, excuse-making and settling for “good enough.” The culture came first, and the results followed. McLaren went on to win back-to-back Constructors’ Championships in 2024 and 2025, along with Lando Norris’s first Drivers’ title. When standards slip, the damage rarely shows up on the P&L right away. Instead, it works like a hidden tax, gradually slowing the company down and making its work less clear and less consistent. Low standards let small compromises slide: a late deliverable here, an unresolved conflict there, a small cut in product quality to hit a deadline. Each one looks minor on its own. Together, they wear down a company’s competitive edge and weaken its brand. Consistently high standards across every department have the opposite effect. When employees know excellence is the baseline, they hold each other accountable, which reduces the need for constant management oversight. Managers spend less time fixing avoidable mistakes and more time on strategy and innovation. Sales teams can focus on better-fit, higher-margin clients because the brand isn’t built on competing on price alone. In short, high standards can improve your bottom line by cutting the hidden costs of rework, lost customers and repairing a damaged culture. To put these ideas into practice, build the following steps into how you run your business: When leaders get disciplined about what they let into their organizations, they stop reacting to problems created by low-quality inputs and start protecting what matters most. With the right standards in place and consistently enforced, results depend less on luck and more on the strength of the organization built to produce them. Ranting about "transgenderism" in Congress, U.S. Senator Thomas "Tommy" Tuberville (R—Alabama) briefly diverted his attention to a different group: furries. "Many" airline pilots, flight attendants, and air traffic controllers, he said, are part of the furry community. If the thought represents a masterclass in the unprovable and unfalsifiable, it's one that's clearly been on his mind; Tuberville did not identify a source for his claim. Tuberville cited several shootings and attempted shootings, including the 2024 attempt to assassinate Donald Trump, the 2023 Covenant School shooting in Nashville and the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. He argued that the perpetrators' gender identities or connections to transgender and furry communities were relevant to the violence. He presented no further proof or evidence. Furries are people interested in anthropomorphic cartoon animals and adjacent topics, and furry fandom ranges from television shows to role-playing games and a vast and ever-growing body of literature. The largest furry convention in the world is Anthrocon, which draws more than 20,000 attendees to Pittsburgh each summer, replete with a spectacular costume parade. There does not appear to be any detailed breakdown of the professional makeup of furry fandom and a quick review of parade footage revealed no anthropomorphic foxes, wolves, cats, etc., in attire consistent with a career in aviation. Research shows furry fandom is not concerned primarily with sexual or gender-related activities, reports the Montgomery Advertiser. The implication here seems to be that Tuberville has some ultra-online staffers obsessed with that sort of thing, or that he is himself sufficiently Internet-poisoned to have taken a personal interest. Tuberville is retiring from the U.S. Senate after a single term and running instead to be governor of Alabama. Though polls put him ahead of incumbent Doug Jones, a rare red-state Democrat leader that he has already beaten once, they're tighter than Republicans want to see in a state that broke for Trump by 31%. Jones said Tuberville's speech was "one of the strangest" he'd ever heard. I had hoped to find at least one stock or appropriately-licensed furry pilot, but concluded my search upon encountering this very good boy posted by Australian national carrier Quantas in 2015. I'm sure it was a ruff flight! ChatGPT sent 95.1% of AI referral traffic to websites in August, BrightEdge data shows. Its referrals doubled this year, while Claude and Perplexity fell. ChatGPT sent 95.1% of the traffic that AI chatbots referred to websites in August, its highest share this year, according to new data from BrightEdge. The search marketing company said referral traffic from ChatGPT grew 101% between January and August. Gemini came second in August with 2.4%, BrightEdge said. Perplexity had 1.1% and Claude 0.8%. ChatGPT sent about 22 times as much traffic as the three combined. ChatGPT’s referral traffic rose 36% in August alone, its biggest monthly jump of the year. Gemini grew 1% over the same month, while Claude fell 15% and Perplexity 17%, according to BrightEdge. AI tools still send far fewer visitors to websites than search engines do. But total referral traffic from AI platforms has grown about 73% in less than a year, the company said. “What stands out now is that ChatGPT isn’t simply taking that share back. It is also sending substantially more users to the web than it was at the beginning of the year,” said Jim Yu, BrightEdge’s chief executive and co-founder. BrightEdge linked the rebound to OpenAI’s push to improve ChatGPT after Sam Altman declared a “code red” in December. Early this year, its data showed users switching quickly to whichever chatbot looked most advanced. ChatGPT’s lead shows up in BrightEdge’s other data. In June, the company found that OpenAI accounted for 96% of live AI agent activity on the web, meaning visits AI makes on a user’s behalf. OpenAI also made about half of the visits AI crawlers make to train models and build search indexes. BrightEdge also found that AI agents now make about 88 requests for every 100 visits from ordinary search. Other trackers have seen a more crowded market. Similarweb found in July that AI search is fragmenting across more assistants. Gemini reached a billion monthly users in August, and ChatGPT hit that mark in June. BrightEdge sells tools that help brands track how they appear in ChatGPT and other AI engines. Its earlier research found that Google’s AI cited Facebook in 19.5 million answers. 30th CelebrationPokÃ©mon TCGPrice Guide  The PokÃ©mon TCG’s 30th Celebration set is causing all sorts of entertaining consternation in the wake of its excellent pull-rates. As scalpers and resellers start falling apart, future releases and reprints of the set look likely to be more easily available for regular customers, meaning enthusiasts and younger players will finally be able to get their hands on the cards they want to keep the most. This means that, rather than multiple cards selling for prices in the high hundreds as with recent sets like Ascended Heroes, 30th Celebration has already settled to sub-$100 prices for most of its top cards (outside of the classic collection), and those’ll keep coming down. The trend for the last couple of years, including the end of Scarlet & Violet and the current run of Mega Evolution sets, has been for scalpers to scoop everything up immediately, thus boosting the resale market to ridiculous places in a set’s first month on sale. Some of those inflated prices stick, like with Ascended Heroes, Destined Rivals, and Prismatic Evolutions, but others eventually settle to slightly more sensible places such as with Perfect Order, Chaos Rising, and Pitch Black. So, as ever, if you’re looking to buy singles, either for a collection or a show-off deck, always wait at least a month before paying, maybe two. We’re talking a difference of literally hundreds of dollars. What makes 30th Celebration so fascinating is that it’s dropped to those same sorts of prices within just days, and it looks like they’ll keep coming down. The most expensive card in the main set is the Mew ex Special Illustration Rare, and that’s “only” $152 at the time of writing. Given that most recent sets have seen their top card at well over $1000 within the first couple of weeks at least, this is a dramatic difference. There’s a twist when it comes to the Classic Collection, a subset of 30 cards featuring all-time favorites with a new “30th” stamp. They’re proving tougher to pull than people were expecting, and as such are seeing higher prices. The Crystal Lugia is currently riding high at $280, impressively beating the holo Charizard of legend at $185. But again, after the Magikarp at $107, the other 27 are all below $100 already (including Gengar Prime!), with some like poor old Misty from Base set at just $10. Meanwhile, the splendid Buzzwole GX manages just five bucks! There is an exception to these lower prices, however: the infamous RGB Mews. These are three cards that have gone entirely unmentioned in all official documentation, and have yet to even be acknowledged as real by The PokÃ©mon Company, making them entertainingly mysterious, and all the more so thanks to their scratchy, knock-off-looking design. They’re also extremely rareâso much so that pull-rates on the three cards, one red, one blue, one green, have yet to be calculated. (There’s a rumor that the PTCG Live digital version of the card pulls one in 10,000.) However, a fair few of the oddities have already been sold on eBay, and the average price is around $4,000. With all that said, we’re putting together the top 15 highest-priced cards nice and early after this set’s release, because most are already pretty affordable. Still, I do suggest waiting a couple more weeks before buying any, because I feel confident these prices will come down by perhaps another half. This ranking combines both the main set and the Classic Collection, because they’re all in the same packs, and therefore we’re bumping this up to 15 entries from the usual 10. Originally from 2002’s Neo Destiny, Shining Celebi maintains enough affection to currently be going forÂ $46. There’s only one Tag Team card in the Classic Collection, and rather boringly they opted for Pikachu & Zekrom GX. It could have been Latias & Latios GX! (Which currently sells for $4,500.) Or a Rainbow Rare Mewtwo & Mew GX! ($450). Given all the Pikachus already in the packs, it was an odd choice to reprise this one from Sun & Moon’s Team Up back in 2019. The original sells for $53 at the moment, and this new version is fetching…$53. Spooky. What a glorious explosion of color from artist You Iribi. Everyone’s favorite trans icon, Sylveon, is selling for $65. These Future Rare cards were originally selling for $3,000 ahead of the set’s official launch, and were hyped by “investors” as the big money. So it’s rather hilarious that the Mewtwo Future Rare is currently only getting around $72. This card, the Gengar Prime from 2010 Heartgold & Soulsilver set Triumphant, still hits hard. If you pulled one of those originals you’d be sitting on $570 (and $14,400 in a PSA 10), but this new version sells just now for $79. There are two Pikachu ex Special Illustration Rares in the set, which is a touch confusing. One is set in the daytime, the other at night, and the latter is proving more popular. Both are completely wonderful, of course, thanks to gorgeous art from Kantaro, packing in as many pocket monsters as possible onto a small card. Pull this and you could sell it for $81. In any other set of the last two years, a Mewtwo this stunning would easily be selling for $300 or more, so it’s incredible to see this masterpiece by Yano Keiji at only $85. If any card is going to hold its value, I’d say it’s this one, likely to be worth a couple of hundred in a couple of years. But far better as a trophy in a binder. The truism that says “make a PokÃ©mon card’s background detailed enough and it’ll gather riches” proves true yet again. (It’s a truism now that I’ve said it, at least.) Akira Egawa, the absolute master of these incredibly detailed pieces of art, does it again with Jirachi, and the card is selling for $101. Future Rare Mew ex might be going forÂ $103, but that still remains far lower than the $3,000 people had been hyping. Gosh, anyone who actually paid that over the last couple of weeks must be unable to get out of bed. Also, it’s incredibly stupid-looking. You can see why the nighttime version is more popular, can’t you? The same artist packs in even more creatures this time, including Snorlax, Zapdos, Meowth and Umbreon, among so many others. It’s a fan-favorite festival. $103 is still far too much to pay for it, but given it’s Pikachu, there’s a chance the price won’t fall far lower in the immediate future, although that depends on how many more flood the market. I kind of love that TPC picked Shinji Kanda’s Magikarp from all the cards he’s created. They could have gone for the wildly popular Giratina V, but instead the dumb ol’ fish got a well-deserved place in the Classic Collection. This was originally part of 2023’s Paldea Evolved set, and the original sells for a mighty $370. This stamped version falls a long way behind at $107. This is so awesome. What a lovely piece of cartoon art, with incredible background work and a cheeky Gengar up to no good. Artist Choriso is very new to PokÃ©mon card art, with only four cards illustrated so far, and incredibly this is her first full art ever. What a way to make an entrance. The card’s market value is currently $126. Here’s the top card outside of the Classic Collection, and you can see why. Mew is the star of the 30th Celebration, despite Pikachu appearing in every pack, and this astonishing art by Kuroimori deserves to be proving so popular. They’ve given us some of the best full arts in recent years, like the Surging Sparks Feebas, and Paldean Fates’ Gardevoir. Right now, you can buy this Mew for aroundÂ $150. Well, this is a bit boring, isn’t it? It’s perhaps unrealistic that TPC would have left the one card to rule them all out of yet another collection of classic cards, but it still feels overdone. At this point you could fill a binder page just with versions of this identical card, although you’d have to be fairly rich. A Base Set shadowless version goes for $2,250 raw, with the Legendary Collection reprint at $900. Base Set 2’s version can get around $500, XY Evolution’s is $103, the 25th anniversary Classic Collection is $160, and on and on and on. This one, right now, is fetchingÂ $185, and while it’ll likely drop in the next couple of months, I expect it’ll be back up around that in years to come. Bless the Crystal Lugia for being more wanted than yawnsome Charizard. And how. It’s currently priced at $280, by a stretch the most expensive card in the regular cards, although considerably cheaper than the $4,500 you’d need to pay for an original from 2003’s Aquapolis. We can’t leave these out. There’s no real data on the mysterious (and utterly hideous) so-called RGB Mews, because they’re proving incredibly rare. Perhaps 1 in 10,000, maybe even rarer than that, but they’re not showing up in the pull-rate data from all the usual suspects because their sample sizes tend to be limited to 5,000 packs. However, they are selling on eBay, and I’ve found a bunch of confirmed sales, mostly at around $4,000. It’ll be interesting to see what happens with these, but they could go on to be some of the most expensive cards in the franchise’s history in ten years’ time. When a client calls the mid-market consulting firm West Monroe to discuss supply chain efficiency, it doesn't start by preparing a slide deck for the first meeting. Instead, it builds a customized app using AI to start the conversation. "No one's ever been inspired or moved or woken up excited about a PowerPoint," Bret Greenstein, West Monroe's chief AI officer, told Business Insider. "And yet so much of consulting is to produce a PowerPoint to compel or convince or persuade somebody." Founded in Chicago in 2002, West Monroe has about 2,000 employees. Since adopting its app-first approach in January, the firm has brought a working demo or app to about a third of first client conversations. The firm builds the apps to give clients a concrete look at how AI could change their work. Greenstein said the approach addresses two familiar problems: Consulting firms can spend too long polishing PowerPoint presentations without helping clients visualize what comes next, while pilot projects can take weeks to fund and build without leading anywhere. The aim is to collapse the traditional deck and proof of concept into a single step: a working product. For a ​ telecommunications company seeking help with its supply chain, West Monroe first used AI to find publicly available information about its suppliers, business priorities, and technology stack. It then applied its own supply chain expertise to envision how an agent-powered system could work. Instead of simply describing that concept in the first meeting, the firm built a prototype tailored to the client. The app used the client's branding and synthetic data designed to reflect its operations. The idea is to make the proposal feel tangible, like sitting in a car at a dealership and picturing yourself owning it, Greenstein said. The client liked it but wanted to see hardware, software, and services together. West Monroe changed the app during the meeting. The demos are not final products. Greenstein said a client still needs integration, data work, process changes, and change management before it can use the software in its business. AI has made it faster to build an early version. Greenstein said that the firm uses a variety of public AI tools like ChatGPT Work and Codex, Claude Code, Google AI Studio, and Antigravity, among others. Before they adopted an app-forward approach, he said it would take about eight weeks to build something like this. Now the team can create the first demo version in roughly an hour. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    West Monroe has an internal app store with more than 700 apps and templates based on client work. The firm has been able to reuse examples 30 or 40 times, Greenstein said, adjusting them incrementally for a new client's systems and data. The approach helps move client conversations beyond the question of whether the firm can build an AI tool. Right off the bat, they can discuss whether the company has the right data, how workers will use the technology, and what may need to change for it to work. "Outcomes, outcomes, outcomes," Greenstein said. "I don't think anyone really cares about AI for the sake of AI." No comments right now, check back later. Comments are unavailable right now. Jump to
