Back in 2018, Maekaeda Gibbons was a loan officer at Bank of America, spending her days evaluating other people's finances. She had a problem: an expensive taste in perfume that didn't match a loan officer's salary. So she started experimenting with her own versions of pricier scents, with no real plan beyond wanting something that smelled good, cost less, and maybe she could use as gifts for coworkers and friends. "I had some funds left over after I paid all of my bills, and I wanted to take a risk on myself," Gibbons told Business Insider. She took around $300 and went into her kitchen to cook up a scent she could fall in love with. Gibbons spent about $54 on bottles she ordered off Amazon, and the remaining money was spent on carrier oils, or oils used as a base for fragrances, for testing formulas. What started as a hobby turned into a paid side hustle once word spread around the office and people started asking to buy it themselves. Seven years later, Brown Sugar Babe earned $21 million in gross revenue, according to digital sales dashboards and financial records viewed by Business Insider. It also has a flagship store in Atlanta, a cult following on TikTok, and no outside investors. Here's how she did it. Gibbons has never raised outside money for the company, and to her, that fact explains most of how the business actually runs. The tradeoff, Gibbons said, was speed. Self-funding forced the business to stay lean and grow slowly, with some ideas kept on the back burner until there was enough capital to pursue them. "As a business owner and even not having the capital, I really had to go off of vibes, and I know that sounds really irresponsible," she said. And by "vibes," she means leaning hard into what customers say they want (she runs surveys asking her social media community what to make next), then figuring out how to pay for it after the fact, not before. "If it meant I had to max out a credit card to accomplish getting the ingredients, raw materials, and vessels that were needed to do that, that's what I did," she said. When Brown Sugar Babe needed to stock up on roughly two years' worth of inventory and ingredients, Gibbons made several purchases over about three months, totaling about $5.5 million, she said. She looked into financing the purchase, then decided to pay for it outright over time. "I really wanted to stay safe with our nest," Gibbons said. It was extremely stressful at first, but Gibbons said that knowing the raw materials for the next two years were locked in let her focus on execution rather than worrying about supply chain volatility. Though she's extremely open to experimentation, there's one category Gibbons won't touch: alcohol-based eau de parfum. "There's a small hard no for several reasons on going into EDP, atomized perfumers or alcohol based perfumes," she said. "It's been done and overdone and continues to be done very well by other brands." A lot of Brown Sugar Babe's lineup is built around notes pulled from established luxury scents, and Gibbons said so openly. She just doesn't love the word people reach for when they speak on it — dupe. She doesn't start from a specific luxury bottle and set out to copy it. In her telling, it starts with loving a scent, then figuring out how to make it louder. It does come with risk. For example, in 2024, Sol de Janeiro sued MCoBeauty, alleging false advertising, trade-dress infringement, and unfair competition. The company claimed that MCoBeauty's fragrance mists copied the look and feel of its Cheirosa body-mist line, including the notes, packaging, and branding. MCoBeauty pushed back, filing a motion in January 2026 to dismiss, arguing that the suit amounts to an attempt to block a lawful competitor. The case is still pending in federal court. Gibbons thinks the criticism looks different depending on the brand. "Are you going to be mad with someone who made macaroni and cheese the same way that you made macaroni and cheese?" Gibbons said. And other brands have started duping her formulas, so she knows what it's like to be on the other side. She said that part doesn't bother her, though. "Everyone needs inspiration," she added. Many fragrance brands stay online and skip the overhead of a physical space, but Gibbons wanted a physical touchpoint for customers who valued in-person connection, which she felt her digital presence alone couldn't provide. After years of building the brand, Gibbons opened a flagship store in Atlanta in 2025, and the investment totaled about $1.2 million, including construction, branding, and the grand opening event. "Sometimes I want to do so much more when it comes to giving our community something that they will remember," she said, talking about how she ensures the brand hosts IRL, including live events and pop-ups. "Even bridling my imagination when it comes to our experiences has been a little tough to take sometimes." Gibbons has also been wrong about how much people want what she's selling. Brown Sugar Babe has sold through entire launches more than once, and website crashes are a familiar headache at this point. Have you ever taken a photo on your phone, only to look back later and wonder where all the life went? I've seen people ask why their newer smartphone photos look dull and sterile compared to their older phone, and the answer mainly lies in how phones process photos these days. Google seems to have heard everyone's cries and implemented a new feature on the Pixel 11 series called Camera Looks. These looks are more than a plain filter; they change how color science works and how shadows are calculated when you take a photo, leading to a result you'll hopefully like better.      To understand what Camera Looks does to your photos, you first have to understand how modern smartphone photography works. Unlike a "normal" camera, modern smartphones don't just take one picture when you tap the shutter button. Instead, your Pixel phone constantly takes pictures while the camera viewfinder is open; it just doesn't store them until you tap the shutter button. The moment you press the shutter button, your Pixel saves roughly five photos taken before you press it, plus another five taken during and slightly after. Each photo is taken at different exposure values — meaning some photos are darker while others are brighter — to ensure the camera captures the widest range of light in an image. All this happens in less than a split second. Your Pixel then takes those photos and combines them into a single picture at the pixel level. If you've ever taken a photo and then immediately tapped the thumbnail to see your shot, you've probably seen the picture "pop" into place and look a lot better after a second or two. This is the result of what Google calls HDR+.      While brightening the shadows and reducing the brightest parts of the photos might be technically excellent, it doesn't look "correct" to our eyes. After years of developing HDR+ into the industry's most technically advanced photo-processing software, Google is letting users pull back on the proverbial reins if they want to. Google calls this extra control "Camera Looks," and it gives users a quick, easy way to make the Pixel camera look and work the way they want. You can reduce or enhance any specific processing parameters, including sharpening, shadows, vibrance, tinting, and more. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Camera Looks aren't "filters." Each look changes how the photo is processed when taken and delivers a different end look. A filter is something applied to a photo after it's taken, while Camera Looks changes the entire processing pipeline. Camera Looks is supported on all Pixel 11 series phones, including the base Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google hasn't ported this feature to older Pixel phones yet, as Camera Looks currently runs at the hardware level on the Tensor G6's ISP. Camera Looks is a simple feature on the surface, but it also lets power users dive into more granular settings. Here's how to apply basic Camera Looks to your photos: 1. Open the camera app. You can also double-press the power button to quickly launch the camera. 2. Tap the Settings Sliders button on the bottom right of the viewfinder. 3. Tap on the Looks button on the bottom left of the viewfinder. 4. The viewfinder will now transform into a series of cards. At the top, tap the dropdown next to "default look" and select your desired base processing style. 5. You can also swipe through the Camera Looks cards to choose from 7 different preset options.      By default, you'll need to tap the Camera Looks button every time you reopen the camera. Google does this to make "normal" photo-taking easy, but you can also set your preferred camera look as the default when you open the camera. To do that, follow these steps: 1. Open the camera app. 2. Tap the photo settings icon on the bottom left. It looks like a gear. 3. Tap the More button on the top right of the pop-up. It looks like three dots. 4. Scroll down and enable Always use selected look.      Now, when you open your Pixel's camera, the Camera Look you previously configured will always be enabled. To disable it, just tap the Camera Look button on the bottom right, then swipe through the cards to select another look.      While the carousel of cards is a quick way to get some nice presets, Camera Looks lets you dial in eight different properties of the Pixel's photography engine and adjust them in granular detail. When you open Camera Looks, you'll see a row of buttons along the bottom for individual settings. Here's what each one does: Contrast (-10 to +10): The difference between the image's brightest and darkest parts. Increase this number to create starker darks and lights, and lower it to make the image gentler. Highlights (-10 to +10): This refers to the brightest parts of a photo, usually something like sunlight coming through a window, a reflection in glass, etc. Increase this number to brighten highlights, and decrease it to reduce them. Shadows (-10 to +10): This setting affects the darkest parts of a photo. Increasing this number brightens all the dark parts in an image. Decreasing this number will make the darker parts even darker, resulting in higher-contrast scenes. Vibrance (-10 to +10): This setting affects color intensity. Higher vibrance settings make colors "pop" but can look unrealistic or cartoony at too-high settings. Lower settings make colors look duller. Tint (-10 to +10): Adjusts how green or magenta an image is. Higher numbers skew the image toward a more magenta tone, while lower numbers make the image look greener. Warmth (-10 to +10): Adjusts how blue or yellow an image is. Higher numbers skew the image toward yellow, or warmer colors, while lower numbers skew the image toward blue, or cooler tones. Sharpness (0 to 15): This refers to how much artificial sharpening is added to a photo. Digital photography often uses sharpening to make photos look "high resolution" by enhancing fine detail, but an image that's too sharp looks noticeably fake and often "harsh." Grain (None/Weak/Moderate/Strong): Adds an artificial grain look to photos. This differs from digital noise, a by-product of how digital photo sensors work. The grain setting does not enhance fine detail. It only adds a grain filter.      Feel free to play with each of these settings to find the look you want. If you don't like the look of stock Pixel photos, I suggest adjusting three settings right away: shadows, vibrance, and sharpness. Try dropping the shadows a notch or two and see if you like the look. I think the preset "Shadows" Look (found in the drop-down menu at the top of the viewfinder when Camera Looks is enabled) already does a good job of adjusting this setting. When you're done with that, try giving vibrance a little punch-up. Start with +2 and adjust from there. That, combined with shadow darkening, should give your Pixel photos a nice pop. Lastly, try reducing sharpness just a bit by bringing it down to 8 (the default is 10). This will reduce sharpening, making the photo look more like film and less digital. AMC CEO Adam Aron called Robinhood's tokenized AMC shares a "quasi-fake market" and threatened legal action. Robinhood’s Vlad Tenev pushed back, saying a public company does not get to approve every product built on its stock. In the wake of their social media dust-up, an argument over which kind of token is legitimate has ensued: a wrapped token, which is a claim on the underlying share, or an issuer-sponsored token registered with the transfer agent. The SEC issued a view on Sept. 17, granting a five-year exemption that lets tokenized U.S. stock trade onchain in the U.S. only where the token carries the same dividends, votes and class rights as the share. Synthetic exposure like Robinhood’s tokenized stock is excluded. Across seven sessions between August 31 and September 9, Robinhood’s AMC token closed within 0.87% of AMC’s NYSE close price at the median, and 2.71% at the widest, as measured in the Uniswap pool that carries around 95% of its trading. While the underlying market is open, the price remains largely aligned. However, a different picture emerges when the underlying market is closed. Leading up to midnight on Thursday, September 3, Robinhood’s AMC token went from $2.55 to as high as $23.16, which is nine times the $2.54 AMC had closed on NYSE seven hours earlier, before coming back down to $3.26 within the same hour. Volume through the pool during the hour was $10.5 million.  Wrapped tokens such as Robinhood’s AMC are often structured as claims against offshore issuers, which collateralize the tokens with the underlying shares. Theoretically, if the issuer ensures that underlying stock positions and the claims are matched 1:1, the price should align, but in practice, the two instruments are traded separately and can thus diverge. Arbitrageurs, such as high-frequency trading firms and market-making desks, step in to keep markets in line, lock in arbitrage profits, and close any dislocations. The same mechanism keeps depositary receipts aligned with their underlying shares, and ETFs with their net asset value. In Robinhood’s case, however, the Jersey issuer names only one authorized participant able to create and redeem. The spike fell well inside the hours when it was permitted to do so, but the participant did not mint or burn any tokens at the time. Onchain data shows 47 mints on Friday, Sept. 4, every one between noon and 7 p.m. ET, comfortably inside the cash session, half a day after the token had depegged and recovered. In a functioning market, a dealer can sell short or sell from their own inventory to capture the premium and replenish later. With no infrastructure to borrow tokens, the only way to access new tokens is pre-funding with the issuer. That means buying the share first, but if the NYSE is shut, the broker would have had to buy before market close. Hedging that exposure costs capital for a premium capped by how much the onchain pool can absorb. It’s a proprietary bet with the firm’s capital, not arbitrage. At the issuer level, minting without a share would leave the issuer owing shares it has not bought, carrying risk on its own book until the opening bell, which is not palatable for an instrument that is distributed under the premise of full collateralization. So, the sellers that brought the spike down were holders taking profit. The money circulated inside the token market; no actual shares changed hands. Nobody was arbitraging; everyone involved was making a directional bet with their own capital at risk. None of it had anything to do with the actual AMC share. Hours after Aron's post, a memecoin launched, quoted in tokenized AMC. As demand for the meme token rose, the pool sold AMC tokens to buy it, taking the stock token’s price with it. An instrument built to reference a share in a cinema chain was priced by demand for a memecoin. Every downstream consumer of that price inherited a number generated by unrelated speculation. To limit the effects of price dislocations on the underlying stock, the SEC’s exemption caps onchain trading at 0.25% of the large-cap stock's average daily volume, and 2.5% for all other listed stocks. Wrapped tokens issued offshore to non-U.S. holders, Robinhood’s included, fall outside SEC jurisdiction and carry on as is. Wrapped tokens have demonstrable utility, especially in emerging markets where access to US equities is restricted or expensive. Robinhood's Stock Tokens cover more than 190 companies across 120 countries; xStocks and Ondo do the same job through different plumbing. Outside the U.S., the model requires no agreement from the issuer, no entry on the shareholder register, and no authorization in each market. That is the source of its reach, and of the counterparty risk the holder carries. The wrapped token expands distribution at the expense of potential dislocations from the underlying price, as well as investors’ rights and issuer transparency. The constraint is not Robinhood's schedule, or any other issuer's. In reality, price discovery does not stop when the NYSE or Nasdaq do; many brokers, retail and institutional, remain operational off-hours and accepting order flow from takers on- and off-shore of the U.S., hedging out their risk with overnight venues and derivatives. However, the ability to source the underlying shares in size is severely diminished when the primary exchanges are closed. So the holder has a claim but no market to convert it outside of the NYSE’s regular session, which runs only 32.5 out of 168 hours in a week. Outside market hours, the premium between the token and the share's last close is a risk the buyer carries and pays for when the price converges at the open. The issuer-sponsored model tokenizes the registered share, with the issuer and its transfer agent involved in the transaction. In addition to all the 24/7 and programmable benefits that a wrapped token offers, the IST is the security, with voting rights and corporate actions. That changes the risk market makers are asked to carry. Quote a wrapped token at 3 a.m., and your inventory is a claim on a share, with no live price to reference. Quote an IST and the inventory is the security itself: the print is a transaction in the stock. That does not automatically make any price informative; a thin book at 3am is still a thin book. What it removes is the conversion risk between two different instruments and the counterparty risk of the intermediaries in between. What the IST doesn’t gain is reach outside its own regulatory perimeter, in contrast with the wrapper. The wrapper's distribution comes from being a different instrument in a lighter regime; the IST’s integrity comes from being the share itself. Today, however, ISTs are few and far between. Only a few names trade, Bullish’s BLSH included, and liquidity is thin. The AMC argument has been about who is allowed to issue a stock token onchain. The harder question is how to build a market beyond issuance. The depth of the wrapper market is bounded by a gated conversion between two different instruments keeping two different clocks. The IST removes that bound: with the right infrastructure, genuine price discovery can happen at any hour, on any licensed venue, by a permitted class of participants rather than a handful of appointed firms. The issuer-sponsored token serves the regulated market; the wrapped token gives exposure to those outside it. Run both at once, and both benefit. The wrapper market gets the two things it lacked at 11 p.m.: a live price reference, and an instrument a market maker can arbitrage against. The issuer-sponsored market gets flow from arbitrageurs holding the tokens as inventory to make markets in wrapped tokens. Collateralize the wrapped token with an IST, and the creation and redemption sit on the same rail, settling in seconds, no longer depending on the cash market to source shares. That is when the two stop trading as separate markets and start being parts of the same infrastructure, serving different use cases. The conversation should now focus on how to narrow spreads for market participants trading at 3 a.m., how to shorten the conversion between different instruments, how to clear a continuous market, and who builds the plumbing in between. No one firm can build the entire infrastructure needed. Exchanges, brokers, fund managers, market makers, transfer agents and clearinghouses each hold one piece, and none holds enough alone. Getting them into the same room to build a market is the key objective industry groups like the IST Coalition are trying to achieve. Glass Lewis and Clarity AI have merged, joining a US proxy adviser with a sustainability data and AI company. The combined firm makes Madrid its global centre for AI and data. Proxy adviser Glass Lewis has combined with Clarity AI, which sells sustainability data and AI analytics. The two firms announced the deal on Thursday. The deal closed on 23 September, and no financial details were disclosed. The combined company will make Madrid its global centre for sustainability, data and AI work. It has more than 900 staff in 20 offices, including a new office in Amsterdam, according to the joint statement. “The fact that we are designating Madrid our global centre of excellence for sustainability, data and AI innovation speaks volumes about the strategic importance of the European market and our commitment to it,” said Bob Mann, chief executive of Glass Lewis. Glass Lewis, founded in 2003 and based in San Francisco, advises investors on how to vote at shareholder meetings. It says it serves more than 1,300 investment managers and pension funds. Clarity AI, founded in 2017 by chief executive Rebeca Minguela, sells sustainability data and AI analytics to financial institutions. The firms said it is moving towards authorisation under the EU’s ESG Ratings Regulation. That law has applied since 2 July 2026. ESG rating providers now need authorisation from ESMA, the EU’s markets regulator, to operate in the EU. Providers already active in the EU have until 2 November 2026 to apply. The merged platform will link investment analysis, sustainability, governance, engagement and voting, the companies said. Investors now often handle these in separate systems. Glass Lewis is stronger in the US, and most of Clarity AI’s clients are in Europe, according to the deal’s FAQ. Both firms report client renewal rates above 90%. Minguela said Glass Lewis brings depth in governance and stewardship. That includes key members of the former Sustainalytics team, she said. “Combined with Clarity AI’s technology, AI capabilities, comprehensive sustainability data and sophisticated analytics, this creates a differentiated, integrated platform with deep decision-relevant data and unparalleled expertise,” Minguela said. Europe holds more than 80% of the world’s sustainable fund assets, the companies said. It is still attracting net inflows in 2026. In the US, proxy advisers face growing pressure. In December 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that names Glass Lewis and its rival ISS. It tells the SEC to review its rules for proxy advisers. It also asks the FTC to check whether they break competition law. Glass Lewis said in October 2025 that it will stop issuing its standard benchmark voting recommendations in 2027. It plans to offer voting policies built around each client instead. In January, JPMorgan’s asset and wealth management arm dropped external proxy advisers for its US votes. It now uses an in-house AI tool, Proxy IQ, ESG Dive reported, citing The Wall Street Journal. Other AI companies are also selling to the investment industry. Anthropic has built a Claude tool for advisers, and HSBC Asset Management has invested in AI startup Model ML. Spain is also drawing AI infrastructure money, including a $1bn data centre deal. The firms said existing Glass Lewis and Clarity AI products will continue, with a phased integration. They also said Glass Lewis’ research and voting recommendations will keep the controls needed to stay independent.                                        Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. (Mis)Uses of Technology			  After burning $80 billion on the failed metaverse pivot — and billions more on desperate “me too” offerings in the AI space — Meta is looking to leverage its massive ad dominance to colonize the agentic AI (or personal assistant) market. So they recently introduced Muse, an AI agent represented by cutesy and personalized avatars, capable of doing semi-complex tasks like booking appointments and shopping.  The capabilities and novelty of the agent, as usual, tend to overshadow the potential privacy threats of giving unethical companies access to even more personal accounts and data. And right on cue, security researchers found a massive zero-day flaw in Muse that allowed any app or terminal command to gain access to the authentication token linking users to their Muse account.  That not only created potential access to the Muse account (and everything it had access to in turn), it allowed for user surveillance that wasn’t transparent to the Muse user. Great stuff! Meta marketing had spent a lot of time claiming they’d kept security and privacy at the forefront of Muse’s design so it was a bit of an embarrassing launch. And it certainly didn’t assuage fears about giving big companies like Meta access to even more personal information and login data: “To me, the bar is infinitely higher in terms of the security of these apps. They don’t have to be perfect, but when you take a look at Muse, it’s like they didn’t, in my opinion, think about security, which is really worrisome,” Wardle said. “At the very least, they should be thinking about security from the very start, and they are just not.” Meta’s adventure in mass-appeal agentic AI also ran into a roadblock when Amazon announced it was banning the agent from shopping on Amazon. Amazon’s announcement, made about 12-hours before Wardle discovered the vulnerability, claimed Muse was an “unauthorized AI agent” that “violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use:” “We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate. This helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience, and it is how others operate including food delivery apps and the restaurants they take orders for, delivery services apps and the stores they shop from, and online travel agencies and the airlines they book tickets with for customers. Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience.” Amazon had already sued Perplexity over its comet browser (though unsuccessfully so far), and taken steps to block shopping agents from both Google and OpenAI. You can see how this could steadily devolve into an annoying walled-garden arms race that erodes the functionality of everybody’s agents. There’s obviously interesting potential in agentic AI (aka software), but like so many other arenas, our failure to enforce antitrust law, and obsession with lobotomizing our regulators, means the market is likely to be dominated by the biggest companies. Companies that already spent the last decade making it clear they have very little ethics. And are keen to anti-competitively ratfuck their way to market domination. Which is to say that Amazon’s blockade of Muse is likely only the beginning. In that sense, the future is going to, in a lot of ways, look very much like the past. It’s also another reason why you’d like to see the sector disrupted by cheaper, on-device, open source, open weighted AI alternatives where ideally the end user gets more transparency, better potential security, and more control.  Instead, I suspect 2027 is going to be heavily dominated by companies like Meta (and Amazon) scaring the government about China, resulting in terrible, protectionist, new AI legislation ghost written by its own lawyers.   	Filed Under: agentic, ai, anticompetitive, bots, competition, muse, privacy, security, shopping   	Companies: amazon, meta  No problem, there’s nothing on Amazon worth buying anymore anyway. The fact that Trump is now talking about “Super Intelligence”, an expression that Zuckerberg is using for years, makes me think that Meta is already heavily lobbying about US models (to justify the $275B spent into AI). “Super Intelligence” sounds exactly like some broad definition of frontier models that will soon defined in an Executive Order as “American Intelligence”, the models exclusively made by American companies on American datacenters using American chips, trained with American values. And Meta will be the first company to proudly offer such a model. To win favor with the WH, the Zuckster was going to go with “Trump Intelligence” until it was pointed out that was a contradiction. “We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Why? Nobody respected content creators’ decisions not to participate when training models, and nobody is respecting customer decisions not to participate by ramming these plagiarist bullshit factories down our throats and grey gooing the Internet. Why are service provider decisions special? What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. And beneath the hood it’s all BS and jank, it seems. It’s worse than that: https://mouse.dev/blog/muse-runtime-export/ How much bigger is the principal-agent problem, when the agent is (a) a dumb machine, and (b) unaccountable for its own actions? An agent can be so dangerous to its principal that in human affairs, principals eternally struggle to stop their agents from double-dealing, embezzlement, frontrunning, and otherwise all manner of treachery.  A human agent is in a prime position to be an insider threat. How much worse is it when the agent has lulzy zero-day exploits—and when the agent, itself, can be neither sued nor jailed, nor effectively punished in any way? Courts must assign liability for “agentic AI” to the legal person of its maker—and, with respect to third parties, jointly and severally to its user, the principal.  The first time that an “AI agent” does serious harm to a third party, both the “AI” company and the “AI” user need to be clobbered with a ruinous damage award. On a philosophic level, here intentionally mixing two distinct sense of “agency”, I question the humanity of meat-puppets who surrender their agency to robots.  Worst of all, the meat-puppets are surrendering their agency to products whose makers not only anthropomorphize machines, but also directly dehumanize humans; cf. Sam Altman’s infamous profession of cult faith (@sama, 2022-12-04), “i am a stochastic parrot, and so r u”.  The “AI” industry as a whole disdains creatures who are made of meat.  They are hostis humani generis, almost self-declared.  Beware their sci-fi siren song.    Which is to say that Amazon’s blockade of Muse is likely only the beginning. In that sense, the future is going to, in a lot of ways, look very much like the past.  …in that Amazon has been full of obvious salesbots for at least a decade; since long before this most recent “A.I.” craze started, anyway. It was “slop” before we had the term, and still is. Many of the listings have obvious and wild mismatches between their titles, descriptions, pictures, reviews, and URLs, such that it’s obvious no human ever looked at them (or they’re still-uncaught attempts at fraud). Also, if you search for a type of product and don’t want to deal with picking one—you’d need to advance two or three pages to get past the ads anyway—Amazon’s own bot will give you “Amazon’s choice”. (Assuming the search works at all; I get “something failed on our end; try again” about a third of the time. It’s gone unfixed for years; does Amazon even have humans looking at whether their own site works?) And there are “A.I.-generated” review summaries, necessary mostly because Amazon no longer lets people see the actual reviews without logging in. So I think Amazon is mostly upset that they don’t control some of these customerbots, or don’t get a larger cut of the sales. It’s not that they have principled objection to bots buying from bots. Small things won’t happen. Only the rich and powerful get to ignore all the laws that allows it to be possible. Meta openly pirated material and got away with likely billions in theft. You can see how this could steadily devolve into an annoying walled-garden arms race that erodes the functionality of everybody’s agents. Is that meant to be some sort of downside? A complaint? A lone pair of Vans sits atop a pedestal somewhere inside Dover Street Market Paris. Worn down, ripped up, and scribbled on, they look like memories. And in some ways, these Vans are just that. Memories.  But this pair is also one of 150 released by the Berlin-based skatewear label Dagger. Each one has been lovingly, painstakingly, customized to look like the ones from founder Luke Rainey’s childhood in Portrush, Ireland. Set within the luxury boutique’s cavernous basement, the experiential, expansive pop-up also premieres Ghosts, a deeply personal new short film Rainey filmed in Portrush for Fall/Winter 2026, featuring Dagger-clad youths re-enacting Rainey’s own adolescent memories.  The Dover Street Market installation is the culmination of six years of hard work to get the brand off its feet, growing from a small collection of grungy graphic tees into a full-fledged fashion label. It's also the first stop in an international rollout that’ll take Ghosts to Tokyo and Berlin and introduce another custom piece alongside the Vans: a line of 150 Eastpak backpacks covered in handmade illustrations, plus patches by graphic designer Hugo Jalabert, who's worked with everyone from Versace to Louis Vuitton.  The bags will come later — releasing at stockists in Italy, Japan, and South Korea in October — but for now, Dagger’s focus is fully in Paris. During a coffee-and-cigarette break before the DSM Paris pop-up, Rainey sent us a handful of WhatsApp voice notes about the lore behind the Vans and Eastpak collabs, plus the pride (and shock) of seeing his Portrush memories translated into a short film. This interview has been condensed and edited. Portrush has haunted every part of the brand from the start, so Ghosts feels like a natural title. What was it like to finally see these memories onscreen? I look at it with relief and shock that it happened, but also a lot of pride. It was a super difficult process to get this made. I'm in my sixth year of the brand, and I'm still funding it completely on my own, so there usually isn't money for things like making a film. I really had to pull in my community and friends; there were many times when we thought we were going to have to pull it, but it's here.  In a more personal way, it's very confronting. I had a horrendous experience growing up queer there and experienced extreme bullying and extreme isolation. I was completely alone, hence the title Ghosts: I was invisible in a town full of people, and felt like a ghost. Seeing that environment again on screen with the Dagger kids feels like looking at my future and my past combined. It's hard to say how I feel about that, because I don't really understand how I feel myself. I hope that through the film, I'll be able to make peace with past me and future me.  Each pair of Vans leaves the studio already carrying a bit of Dagger spirit. Once someone takes a pair home, what do you hope they add to it? With this shoe in particular, we wanted to promote the idea that footwear — especially limited-edition footwear like this — isn't something to be coveted, put in a glass box somewhere, and kept pristine. It's something to be worn; it should encourage you to live your life in it. We distressed and disintegrated the shoe and dyed it to make it look like it had already had a life and a story.  That story is mine, but as soon as the buyer or wearer puts it on, it becomes theirs. I hope I see someone wearing the shoe in five years' time and it looks completely different from the one we gave them, because it's become theirs. Vans is one of your key collaborators. How has the relationship grown alongside the brand, and what makes this project different? The shoe we're releasing today with Dover Street Market Paris comes from a pair I took to our Paris showroom and sat in the middle of the room — honestly, just to flex that we were working with Vans, because it legitimized the brand at that point. We'd never done a show before, and at that stage we were known more as a T-shirt brand, so I had a lot to prove.  The buyers immediately walked up to the Vans and tried to buy them, so I hit Vans up and told them, "Guys, these amazing tier-one stores are interested in this shoe. Is there something we can do?" That's how we came up with the concept of doing these 150 custom pairs, plus the events around the release. How did the Eastpak collection come about? And why is the backpack such a key part of the collection? It was the same with the Vans: I put an Eastpak backpack in the middle of the showroom, and buyers and customers wanted it immediately. We worked out a deal for 150 bags, and I hit up my friend Hugo to make some amazing patches for the bag. He started off as a customer, and from there we became friends. And then Serena, who works in-house at Dagger, did every single illustration by hand. There’s a lot of our community in those bags. One of my fondest memories is actually my grandmother teaching me how to sew. She was stitching patches on my bag, and I wasn't very good at it because I wasn't very patient — it's kind of hilarious that I've ended up in fashion. So it was important to me to have the Eastpak bag in the show because it was the first time I really started telling the story of that time in my life: as a queer kid, [my backpack] was where I would hide little letters and little notes. I remember I had a CD from a gay guy I met in a club — when I was far too young to be there — of a pop star’s album he'd downloaded from LimeWire. I couldn't show anybody. I kept that CD in my backpack, along with many other things that definitely shouldn't have been in my backpack at that age. Bullish (BLSH), Equiniti, Alpaca, Apex Fintech Solutions and DriveWealth have formed a new industry group focused on building standards for tokenized securities that remain directly tied to the companies that issue them. The Issuer Sponsored Token Coalition, unveiled on Thursday, was convened by CoinDesk parent company Bullish and Equiniti, a shareholder-services and market-infrastructure firm that is being acquired by the crypto platform. The group said they plan to work on technical standards, settlement, custody and ways to move securities between traditional market infrastructure and blockchain networks. Its main focus is issuer-sponsored tokenization, in which a tokenized share would be linked to a company’s official shareholder register. That structure is designed to preserve rights such as voting, dividends and participation in corporate actions. The distinction has gained attention as firms roll out products that offer stock exposure without always giving holders direct ownership of the underlying shares. A recent dispute between AMC Entertainment CEO Adam Aron and Robinhood highlighted that issue, centering on whether synthetic or tokenized products may leave investors with economic exposure to a stock but without the same legal rights as registered shareholders. Issuer-sponsored models aim to narrow that gap by tying the token directly to the issuer’s records. “The architecture we establish now matters and that is why we are bringing together this group of leading firms to chart the course,” said Tom Farley, CEO of Bullish. Alpaca said it plans to contribute to interoperability between traditional securities and onchain markets through its Instant Tokenization Network. "Tokenization creates an opportunity to connect issuers and investors in ways that weren't possible with traditional market infrastructure," said Arush Sehgal, head of digital assets at Alpaca. "Getting it right means preserving shareholder rights and ensuring onchain markets remain connected to the markets they're built on. Apex Fintech Solutions, which provides infrastructure for broker-dealers and other financial firms, said the group could help establish standards that enable tokenized markets to connect with existing systems. The coalition said its work follows last week’s U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission exemption allowing limited onchain trading of U.S.-listed equities under certain conditions. US airline fares rose almost 24% over the past year, making the prospect of cheaper short flights especially appealing. One possible solution: electric planes. For our video series, "The Limit," I recently took a 25-minute flight on Beta Technologies' Alia CX300. The journey used about $5.25 in electricity. A comparable trip in a conventional jet-fuel-powered plane would have cost an estimated 10 times as much in fuel, about $60 Electric aviation has spent decades promising an electric-car-style revolution. Beyond lower costs, electric planes could make short flights quieter and produce no in-flight emissions. Now, one Vermont-based company is facing a crucial test. Beta Technologies is aiming to get its Alia CX300 certified by the Federal Aviation Administration by the end of 2027. The plane has already flown nearly 400 miles on a charge and stayed airborne for over five hours. The question is whether those advantages can translate into a viable business. Other electric-aircraft startups have run into financial trouble after spending years trying to bring aircraft to market. I toured Beta's manufacturing facility, watched how it builds its batteries and aircraft, and flew aboard the CX300 myself. What I saw helps explain why electric planes still aren't regularly carrying passengers, more than 50 years after the first electric aircraft flew — and what Beta has to accomplish over the next year if it wants to change that. Other electric-aircraft companies have already gone under after spending years and billions of dollars trying to bring their planes to market. Beta is taking a vertically integrated approach, building its own batteries, propulsion systems, planes, and charging technology. The company went public in November 2025, raising more than $1 billion. “It was the largest founder-led industrial IPO in history,” Beta founder and CEO Kyle Clark told me. In order to fly about 300 nautical miles, the Alia CX300 must carry nearly 3,000 pounds of batteries. The jet fuel needed to fly a comparable distance would weigh only about 50 pounds. The CX300 can carry just five passengers and one pilot, underscoring how battery weight constrains the size and range of electric aircraft. That's why Beta is initially targeting relatively short routes of about 150 to 200 miles. The CX300's 50-foot tapered wingspan, V-shaped tail, and rear-mounted propeller reduce drag and conserve battery power. Its wing shape was inspired by the Arctic tern, a bird known for its long migrations. During my flight, the pilot shut off the motor, and the aircraft continued gliding without power. With a roughly 17-to-1 lift-to-drag ratio, Beta says the CX300 could glide down to a suitable landing strip after a complete loss of power. While I was inside the aircraft, the sheer acceleration took me by surprise. The CX300 reached roughly 87 knots, about 100 mph, before lifting off, and once we were airborne, the pilot put the plane through a series of sharp rolls and banks. The flight was smooth overall, though the sharp banking was enough to make me a little queasy. I don't blame the electric propulsion: I think that would have happened to me in any small plane. A gas-powered aircraft can land and refuel at airports around the world, while an electric plane needs charging infrastructure to get back into the air. Beta has installed more than 120 charging stations across the US, and its system can recharge an aircraft in under an hour. The company is also building the charging technology itself, meaning it can develop the planes, batteries, propulsion systems, and infrastructure as parts of the same ecosystem. Getting the technology to work is expensive. Beta says it generated a little more than $35 million in revenue last year against about $400 million in operating expenses. The company is also building a business around replacement batteries, which it expects customers to need repeatedly over an aircraft's lifetime. Beta is targeting FAA-conforming production of the Alia CX300, its conventional-takeoff aircraft, at the end of 2026 or early 2027, with certification expected by the end of 2027. The company plans to start with medical, cargo, and defense missions before moving into passenger service, while continuing to develop a vertical-takeoff version that wouldn't need a conventional runway. Electricity itself can be cheap: The CX300 demonstration flight I was on cost only a few dollars in electricity, according to Beta. Commercial operators would still have to pay for pilots, maintenance, insurance, charging infrastructure, and battery replacements. Beta has already shown that an electric plane can fly hundreds of miles. By the end of 2027, it hopes to prove something much harder: that one can make it through certification and become a commercial aircraft. No comments right now, check back later. Meta's looking to make virtual reality a reality … again. The tech giant unveiled a new version of its virtual reality glasses at its annual developers conference, Meta Connect. Before you panic that you've traveled back in time, this isn't quite the same metaverse Mark Zuckerberg was pitching back in 2021. The goal of replacing the hardware in your pocket, though, remains the same. More on that in a bit. Meta VR Glasses, which go on sale next spring, are a far cry from the bulky headsets we typically associate with virtual reality. (I'm looking at you, Apple Vision Pro.) Weighing in at a svelte 100 grams and costing $1,300, Meta VR Glasses are much lighter and cheaper than the Apple Vision Pro, which weighs 600 grams and costs $3,700. But don't take my word for it. BI's Peter Kafka took them for a test drive. He said the difference between Meta VR Glasses and Apple's Vision Pro is immediately noticeable. But, like the Apple Vision Pro, he also struggled to think of many reasons to use them regularly. Read his full review here. The VR glasses weren't the only thing Meta showed off at the event. There was also an update on Meta's somewhat controversial AI glasses, as well as new partnerships with Disney and others to boost entertainment options on its new gadgets. Here are all the highlights from the event. Meta's betting on a future where people won't default to their phones. Muse, Meta's buzzy new personal AI agent, is deeply integrated into the new VR glasses and also got its own palm-sized device users can speak into. It's called Charm, and should be ready to ship for the holidays. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    It's another way Meta can pull you deeper into its ecosystem, and away from your iPhone. Ideally, Zuckerberg would love for users to remain in a Meta-exclusive world: wearing Meta VR Glasses while interacting with Muse, scrolling Instagram and Facebook, and chatting with friends on WhatsApp. He's not alone. The fact that so many of us live on our iPhones is a major bummer to tech companies since it gives Apple an incredible advantage. Currently, Apple doesn't need to stress too much about AI because companies still rely on the iPhone to get their fancy AI products to consumers. It's like running the only toll bridge over a river that sits between two major cities. Even if the road isn't great, or it gets a lot of traffic, it's still the only way to get to where you need to go. (Yes, green-bubble people, Android means there are two bridges over the river. But Apple still holds the majority of the US market share.) AI is such a revolutionary technology that it's viewed as an opportunity to rethink things and find a new path other companies can completely control. Why take the bridge when you can build your own flying cars? Just look around. AI startups are pitching "friends" you can wear around your neck. OpenAI hired Apple design legend Jon Ive and is encouraging people to change how they use their phones. Meta is returning to the VR well after having already sunk $80 billion into it. It's not easy — blazing new trails never is— but there's too much money at stake not to try. The rub, as always, will be getting people to buy in. Users bring developers who'll build apps to grab the audience's attention. But people only come if there is cool stuff to do, and developers are only willing to spend time building if there are people there to use it. Even Apple, the king of hardware, had trouble navigating this with the Vision Pro. Meta could run into the same issues. Peter said he doesn't see many immediate uses for the glasses. Three years ago, Meta launched Threads as a Twitter alternative, staffed with a bare-bones team. Now the company says its text-based social network has 500 million users — more than Twitter ever reported when it was a public company (In 2024, Elon Musk claimed his rebrand of the service had brought in 600 million users.) Another marker of Threads' growth from side-project to Real Thing is that Instagram boss Adam Mosseri, who had been supervising Threads, has handed control of the service to longtime Meta product guy Connor Hayes. I caught up with Hayes at Meta's headquarters this week to talk about Threads' evolution, its stance on AI content — and how Meta is using the strategies it used to grow Threads as it pushes out Muse, its buzzy AI agent. Peter Kafka: When Threads launched in 2023, you were actively courting Twitter users who didn't love what was happening under Elon Musk's ownership. But Twitter is still around. Bluesky has its own user base. Who is a Threads user today? Connor Hayes: We assumed in the very beginning that growing Threads would be predicated on capturing people from these other services. We've actually been able to grow the market. It turns out there were a lot of people that were using Facebook and Instagram every day who are willing to use an app built around this type of text format that hadn't been using alternatives like Twitter before. In the beginning, it was purely, "I'm looking for an alternative." And it felt like a safer, more positive conversational environment. Now it's starting to grow into its own thing that's built around these communities. We're trying to go really deep on categories that people are super passionate about, in a way that I think Reddit has done a good job with in the past. We're trying to get into this space that's a hybrid of what Twitter was, what messaging is and what Reddit has been. A big way you've grown is by promoting Threads to Instagram and Facebook users. Now Meta is using that same playbook to promote Muse. Is promoting a new AI agent to Instagram users different than telling them about a new messaging app? The biggest difference is that Threads is built around user-generated content. The engine that powers our growth today are promotions we do on Facebook and Instagram, where we know that your account is linked and we can recommend you content from Threads on Instagram while you're scrolling. Of course, you're going to be interested in that, because we found a way to match it. For something like Muse, the big challenge is: How do we use what we know about you and your interests and promote this app to you, without having a base of user-generated content that can kind of do that work for us? The tech guy uniform is full of basic T-shirts and bad haircuts, so I get why Alexandr Wang's look at Meta Connect is riling Silicon Valley. If you're used to the black turtlenecks of Steve Jobs and Elizabeth Holmes, or the white T-shirts of Mark Zuckerberg, sure, Wang's camo-print deer T-shirt and matching Crocs seem like a fashion statement. They are not. They are merely how 20-something coastal elites dress these days. I could throw a stone in Bushwick, Brooklyn, and hit seven of these types in one go. Last year, I dated an early-stage founder who insisted on exclusively thrifting his clothes, just as Wang has insisted that his deer-print shirt cost no more than $30 from a Santa Cruz shop. (Thirty bucks for a used T-shirt? The secondhand market has gotten out of control.) For them, wearing only thrift store digs is another badge of honor: Look how hard they're locking in, they won't even spend money on new clothes. Add to that Gen Z's general love of secondhand shopping. Oh, you got that from Shein? Do you want the planet to combust? Despite all the internet sleuthing about how Wang's T-shirt is probably $800 from a designer label, I fully believe that he did, in fact, source it from an overpriced thrift store in Northern California. (I reached out to Meta and Wang, but didn't hear back.) I've spent a significant amount of time in Lake Tahoe, the place whose name adorns the sleeve of his graphic tee. I can confirm the design is exactly the type you'd expect from a place where local bumper stickers read, "Go back to the Bay." Crocs have been hot with Gen Z since at least the pandemic — Piper Sandler found they were the No. 6 favorite footwear brand among teens in 2023, and this year, the brand said it had its first billion-dollar quarter in revenue. Make no mistake: This is a deeply Gen Z-coded outfit. "What's happening with that outfit, whether he means to or not, is he's emphasizing his age," said Daniel James Cole, a fashion historian and professor at New York University. Cole said he's seen students around the campus where he teaches throw on similar fits, matching their outfits to their Crocs to emphasize them. He's not the only one. Sofia Jiang, who works in marketing at clothing rental company BNTO and is the founder of the workwear brand SofSet, said Wang's outfit wouldn't be out of place downtown, where the outfits are zanier. "I would say this is like Lower East Side or Brooklyn, part of a more artistic crowd," Jiang said. She added that she could easily imagine "a 14-year-old boy from LA" picking out the antler camo T-shirt from a thrift store. Gen Z loves ugly and ironic fashion, and other generations love to clown us. Last month, The New York Times ran an op-ed titled, "Gen Z Dresses Like They've Never Worn Clothes Before," arguing that we dress like a pastiche of other subcultures that don't make any sense together. Wang, 29, is following that to T: redneck graphic tee, gorp core fleece joggers, crocs, a mullet straight out of the "Love Island: Australia" villa, and rimless glasses that Ben Franklin himself would've worn. Yes, it doesn't make sense. It's a total mismatch of eras and aesthetics. That's the point. The fact that Wang chose to wear this while presenting at Meta Connect isn't that far off from Zuck's once-radical insistence on wearing the white tee as his uniform. Though Zuck himself has experienced varying levels of drip throughout his style evolution, his dress code has always been casual. Ten years ago, writers waxed poetic on how Zuck helped kill the suit and ushered in the era of business casual. Wang just might be the next iteration of that. Amina Salahou, the founder and creative director of global production network Les Adore, said Wang could be signaling that he's cut from the same cloth of startup founders Meta probably wants on Muse — thrift-shop warriors with no bed frames and passions for agentic AI. "He's just trying to tell the developer community that, you know, he's part of them, he's not part of a bureaucratic system," Salahou said. Most Gen Zers don't have the kind of power or visibility Wang has, which is why he can wear the Gen Z off-duty uniform to speak at a Big Tech developer conference. Meta has revealed slimline VR glasses for immersive entertainment on the go and an audio-only, camera-free version of its Ray-Ban glasses as the latest additions to its expanding product portfolio. Announced by CEO Mark Zuckerberg last night at the technology company's annual Connect conference, the Meta VR Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses expand its market-leading range of eyewear and headsets. The Meta VR Glasses represent the bigger breakthrough, bringing virtual-reality gaming, 3D movies and other immersive digital experiences into a form factor only slightly larger than an ordinary pair of glasses. This allows them to be worn for longer than current headsets and carried on the daily commute, as people might do with a pair of over-ear headphones. Meta says it achieved the lightweight construction by splitting the architecture into two: the glasses, weighing about 100 grams, plus an attached "puck" that clips onto a pocket or bag and handles the processing. Also key are the glasses' ultra-compact pancake lenses, which are about the size of a Scrabble tile and are fixed within a soft mesh structure on the inside of the frames. The wearer manually shifts these lenses to sit directly in front of their eye, filling everything but their peripheral view with a 5K display. This micro-OLED display offers angular resolution of 37 pixels per degree – more than Meta's current market-leading Quest VR headsets and enough to deliver crisp text and rich imagery. The Meta VR Glasses can be used to play games or watch entertainment from the Meta Quest platform, including movies recorded in or converted to 3D. There are also new immersive formats that Meta is pioneering, like "immersive sports" streamed in ultra-high definition from the edge of the playing field at live events. Users navigate the operating system using their eyes, voice and natural hand gestures like swiping and pinching, without having to use controllers – in some cases even to play entire games. Meta also envisions the VR Glasses being used for work. Using full-colour passthrough – the view of the world in front of the glasses that's captured through its outward-facing cameras – wearers can turn any table surface into a keyboard and touchpad and surround themselves with multiple virtual screens from their Mac or PC. The VR Glasses will deliver up to three hours of continuous media playback from the battery on the puck. Meta expects to put the device on sale in spring 2027. Unlike the rest of Meta's eyewear offering, the VR glasses are not intended to be worn all the time or to be used primarily for AI assistance, although the company's new Muse AI will be built-in. The use of Meta's AI glasses out on the street has earned them the nickname of "pervert glasses", due to various documented incidents of men using the barely visible camera to covertly film women. Surveillance concerns were also amplified after a Swedish news investigation revealed that videos captured by wearers' cameras – including highly sensitive ones where they were nude or having sex – were being streamed to subcontractors in Kenya. The pushback against these aspects of the technology may be a driver behind Meta's other key new product launch at Connect, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses. Developed with long-term partners EssilorLuxottica, these glasses lack the controversial camera of other Meta models, as well as the small screen of the Meta Ray-Ban Displays, launched this time last year. Their functionality is more limited, letting users listen to audio through small open‑ear directional speakers built into the frame and interact by voice with Meta's AI assistant. The slimmer feature set has allowed Meta to introduce new slimmer styles like the partially wire-frame Ray-Ban Clubmaster. The glasses' 12-hour battery life and 43-gram weight also mean they can more easily be worn all day. In addition to the new products, Meta revealed the Gen 3 version of its Ray-Ban Meta glasses, with three new frame silhouettes, and several new versions of the cheaper Meta Glasses, launched just three months ago, including one with pop star Lisa, whose influence is partly responsible for the Labubu craze. The keynote presentation also detailed the expanding capabilities of its Muse "personal AI agent", which was first revealed two weeks ago and which the company will be adding to all of its glasses. At the end, there was a quick sneak peek at a new Tamagotchi-like Muse Charm gadget. Meta has established itself as the dominant player in the small but growing market for AI glasses, accounting for 94 per cent of display-less AI glasses shipped in the first half of 2026, according to tracking by Counterpoint Research. By the end of the year, it will have more than 100 different styles available in its Ray-Ban, Oakley and own-brand collections. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 In a bygone era, growth was thought to be an achievement of a company on its own. Now, it’s also commonly a network effect. Platforms, marketplaces and many other businesses depend on ecosystems of freelancers, creators, vendors, contractors, builders and partners to generate demand and deliver value. In Tipalti’s global payments research, 81% of business leaders and entrepreneurs said those partner, creator or affiliate networks were important or critical to their revenue model. For entrepreneurs, it is clear that today’s growth engine goes beyond the confines of an individual organization. The problem: Systems that compensate these partner networks haven’t kept pace with their growing strategic importance. Many companies are still running payouts on infrastructure designed for a simpler era, long before the current digital economy existed. The result is an increasing mismatch between what drives growth and what businesses must invest in to support it. Today, companies face a more fragmented and volatile environment, and that holds true across North America, Europe and Asia. Scaling into new markets adds regulatory entities, tax structures, payment rails and compliance requirements, and those pressures are only accelerating.  In December 2025, McKinsey argued that global operating models must now absorb trade disruption, cybersecurity, regulatory change and data sovereignty, demanding resilient and flexible design rather than tactical patches. In April 2026, BCG named geopolitical and regulatory divergence as a critical risk exposure area for organizations, noting that nearly all surveyed executives cited fast, unpredictable regulatory change as a top external burden. This compounding is where high-growth companies discover an operational breaking point. Rather than a lack of demand, failures occur because complexity exceeds the organization’s ability to manage it. Often, finance and payments absorb that strain first. Late partner payments, fragmented visibility across regions, a growing dependence on manual workarounds and rising audit risk are early signs of a common underlying problem. In the past, the damage from a weak payout infrastructure was easy for companies to ignore: It didn’t appear on any single line of the P&L. Now, that’s changing. In our research, 26% of companies said they lost key partners (from independent contractors and suppliers to creators and contributors) over the past year because of payout-related issues. When partner networks are core to the business, losing them can mean lost revenue with no post-mortem or visibility — an increasing threat to a business’s viability. Internal costs are just as easy to miss. Finance teams in our research reported spending roughly 22% of their weekly capacity on audit preparation and compliance reporting, with another 22% of monthly payouts requiring manual intervention. That recurring strain on time and attention grows with every new market. It can also become a talent problem: 77% of leaders told us operational friction contributes to turnover among their best people. The payment experience is direct evidence of how a company fulfills its commitments to the partners it depends on most. In our research, 93% of leaders said that an unreliable payee experience could damage revenue and, simultaneously, brand reputation. Paying people quickly, accurately, and in ways that work for them is a retention strategy for the ecosystem that drives growth. Still, only 33% of organizations surveyed in 2026 currently view their payout infrastructure as a strategic asset. The rest treat it as an operational function or a cost to be minimized. That gap between how much companies rely on these networks to fuel growth and how they invest in the systems that serve them is one of the most overlooked liabilities in global business today. Growth is now a network effect, and every network runs on payments. That is where the operational breaking point starts, and where it can be prevented. Standardize infrastructure across markets and entities instead of patching each one separately. Build compliance and auditability into every workflow instead of adding them after the fact. Treat the payout experience as the retention strategy it already is, not a cost to be minimized. Three-quarters of organizations in our research expect global transaction volumes to keep increasing, and BCG projects global payments revenue will reach roughly $2.4 trillion by 2029. Growth is coming regardless. The only choice left is whether businesses meet it or break under it. In a bygone era, growth was thought to be an achievement of a company on its own. No matter what industry you're working in or what level you're at, it is indisputable that the job market is tough these days. Hundreds of people at a time apply for the same few positions, companies lie about their salaries and benefits, and job applicants are generally at the mercy of recruiters and potential employers. While unemployment has always been demoralizing, it seems to be particularly bad right now. You might think that the problem ends when you finally secure a job offer, but that couldn't be further from the truth. Some workplaces have all kinds of tricks up their sleeve to ensure what should be a moment of relief and celebration turns into a stressful or just plain confusing incident. Most people expect that the way an employer presents themselves at the interview stage probably isn't going to align with reality completely, but there are levels to this game of professional catfishing. A lot of job seekers have no idea just how insane it can get until they have the misfortune of experiencing it. If only things could be less about weird institutional games and more about hiring legitimate employees. Close-up of a tray with a burger and fries, with a woman putting her fork into the fries and a man behind them. Picture does not depict real parties.  A job applicant was happy to secure a role at a fast food restaurant, or so it appeared. The manager told them that they had got the job, and they were set up on the online portal for employees, where they filled out their information. However, after that, they didn't get any contact from their new employer. There were also no contact details for them to enquire. Today, the internationally known DJ and producer is building Experts Only Festival with Medium Rare, Relentless Beats, and EMW, betting on a new business model that gives artists a stake in the festivals they create. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 With all due respect to our accounting Avengers and the great work they do, it’s hard to believe that most CPAs dreamed of becoming CPAs. That certainly wasn’t the case for John Summit, who went from a monotonous role at Ernst & Young to arguably one of the most exciting careers imaginable: an internationally famous DJ.  Now, in the second year of his Experts Only Festival on Randall’s Island, Summit and his partners at Medium Rare are showcasing a new model for artist ownership, all while bringing the beats. Experts Only is a global movement born from John Summit’s pursuit of total creative freedom. Founded on the ethos of music without limits, Experts Only is embracing genre-defying sound that spans house, melodic, and everything in between. Since its inception, the label has become a platform for talents like Mau P, Kaskade, Odd Mob, Layton Giordani, Cassian, Max Styler, and Summit himself. Experts Only has built its live events around nontraditional venues, including cave shows in Tennessee, mountain events in Vail, Colorado and Lake Tahoe, Nevada, and events in Tulum. The brand has also expanded internationally to destinations such as Ibiza and Amsterdam and has hosted a curated stage at Bonnaroo. Summit found his passion for DJing while studying at the University of Illinois, where he played local shows in his free time. After graduation, he moved to Chicago and took a full-time job at Ernst & Young.  “It was a very soulless job in the sense that I had no fulfillment from it whatsoever,” Summit admits to Entrepreneur, “But the hours are super intense, so I had to have that release of just DJing on the weekends.” For a while, Summit was burning the candle at both ends, grinding through audits during the day while playing local clubs at night.  “None of my coworkers or anything knew,” Summit laughs. “It felt like I was living a double life.” Pretty quickly, Summit’s music started building an online buzz, which was great for his confidence but not so great for his accounting career.  “I started doing worse at work, started showing up later and later and later. I’d come into work with, you know, bloodshot eyes and people would think I was just up all night partying,” he says. “In reality, I was just making the music. Well, I was doing my fair share of partying too for networking, but yeah.” Eventually, Summit quit his job after saving $20,000 to live off while pursuing his DJ dreams, throwing himself into music full-time. Around 2019, things started to take off. Then, the world shut down. Summit moved back in with his parents during COVID-19, but his commitment to music didn’t waver. He kept grinding, and it paid off. Before long, Summit was touring internationally, playing for millions of fans and reaching heights most DJs only dream of. Then, in 2025, he decided it was time to own the brand he had built. That’s where Medium Rare came in. Medium Rare is a $75 million entertainment company built by Forbes 30 Under 30 alumni Joe Silberzweig and Adam Richman. What sets the company apart is its unique 50/50 business model.  “Our model is really simple,” Richman explains. “We’ll take all the financial risk, and we’ll split the profits 50/50.” They used that same model to build Summit’s Experts Only Festival, a two-day music festival that  Summit curated on Randall’s Island. Instead of simply paying an artist to headline someone else’s festival, Medium Rare builds an asset with the artist that both sides own. “We’re going to risk $10 million plus on this event,” Richman shares. “So if it makes $2 million, we each get $1 million. If, God forbid, we lose $2 million, John doesn’t lose a penny.” For Richman, the model works because both sides have a real stake in the event’s success.  “We’ll have people all the time be like, ‘Hey, we’ll work with you in this different model,’” he says. “We’re just like, not for us. We really found this partnership works best for everyone, and it really incentivizes [both sides]. Nothing is fairer than a 50-50, right?” John and his team drive the creative vision and brand, while Medium Rare, Relentless Beats, and EMW serve as partners for the festival. One of the biggest inspirations for Experts Only Festival was an old New York staple: Electric Zoo. “Electric Zoo was a cultural mainstay of New York City. It grew organically for over a decade in the city, got up to, you know, over 75,000 fans or 100,000 fans across the weekend,” Silberzweig shares. “That property was sold, and the new operator didn’t really manage it correctly, and it went bankrupt. So we identified a huge void in the market, and there’s huge demand for these types of events.” Experts Only Festival was built to fill that void, launching the same month Electric Zoo had previously occupied. The inaugural festival brought more than 50,000 fans to Randall’s Island across two sold-out days, and the festival surpassed those numbers in its second year. While Summit may have left the spreadsheets behind, he still carries the business acumen honed from years behind a monitor.  “This is just as much of business as fun,” Summit proclaims. “I mean, if you ask anyone in the team I work with and stuff, like half my day is dedicated to business.”  While some artists balk at the idea of due diligence, Summit finds it oddly comforting.  “I think maybe because I’m used to that from doing the accounting, then doing the music at night, where it’s not fun just doing art 100% of the time,” he shares. “It’s fun to work both sides of the brain.”  He also points out the countless examples of artists getting screwed over because they don’t understand the terms of their deals, and end up going bankrupt.  “How are you making X million dollars a year and then being bankrupt?” Summit wonders. “That’s why you have to have financial literacy. I think having that background makes this kind of stuff possible.” As anyone both financially literate and music festival inclined knows, most of these events don’t turn a profit in their first year, or even the first few. But Summit and Medium Rare are comfortable betting on Experts Only Festival’s long-term success.  “Look at all the best businesses in the world: Amazon, Meta, etc. No one made money in their first couple of years,” Summit says. “And where I’m lucky is that I do well as John Summit, so Experts Only is the true passion project of it all.” Summit has gone through a career change so dramatic that it will almost certainly be the subject of a documentary one day. His advice for anyone considering a similar leap of faith? Have a backup plan, but don’t let it stop you from fully committing. “If you’re gonna do something, you gotta go all in, he says. And so maybe that backup plan is what gave me the mental stability to know that I could go all in. But you can’t half-ass it, though. I think when you do it in your career, and when you hear about anyone who started a successful business or artist career, it’s because they went all in.”  With all due respect to our accounting Avengers and the great work they do, it’s hard to believe that most CPAs dreamed of becoming CPAs. The deepening sell-off in the bond market could soon be a much bigger drag on stocks.  It may not be long before the sell-off rattling government bonds this week spreads to the stock market, Wall Street analysts are warning. Bond turmoil has dominated market headlines this week, with Treasury yields spiking to levels not seen in decades. A grim cocktail of macro, fiscal, and geopolitical concerns has spurred the latest leg down, and investors fear the next shoe to drop will be in the stock market.  Yields influence borrowing costs for a wide range of consumer and business loans, including mortgages, credit cards, and auto loans.  Higher yields also pressure stocks by offering a viable alternative in the form of "risk-free" returns. The thinking goes that locking in a 5% yield for a few years might be preferable to risking money in the equity markets.  Consumers are feeling the pain of higher rates in the mortgage markets, where the average rate on a 30-year home loan broke through 7% for the first time in two years this week.  The warnings are piling up enough for major market commentators to take notice and issue warnings of what might come next.  Steve Eisman, one of the traders made famous by "The Big Short," said a correction is looming unless yields swiftly drop back below 5%. "A market correction seems imminent," Eisman wrote in a note on Substack as the bond sell-off accelerated Thursday morning. "It looks like 5% is the Rubicon for the market. Higher rates increases the deficit. It harms the housing market. And it hurts the AI story, which is now a story partially about leverage," he added, referring to the loads of AI debt being issued by tech giants. Another concern has been that higher yields offered by "risk-free" Treasurys could compete with the bonds being issued by Big Tech firms funding their AI ambitions. If hyperscalers need to sweeten the deal with higher yields to entice investors, it could skew the economics of AI projects at a time when the market is already worried about returns on capex.   Farzin Azarm, a managing director at Mizuho Securities, also flagged the risk of a "serious correction" in the last week, pointing to bond market volatility as one potential factor. "I've been saying this for some time, that eventually the bond market speaks very loudly and the markets will react," he said on CNBC.  Higher yields are just one of several contractionary forces that could slow the economy to a crawl, Jim Paulsen, a veteran Wall Street strategist, wrote in a note on Substack this week. "Expect weaker economic growth, rising recession fears (although probably no actual recession), lower—not higher — bond yields, and a more challenging stock market in the coming months," he said, pointing to tighter financial conditions. Economist Henrik Zeberg said the end of the AI bull market appears to be closer given the moves in bond yields. In a post on Substack laying out his updated markets outlook, he pointed to parallels he sees to 2007.  He said that he's looking for yields to cool off from their current levels to signal a "Blow-Off Top" in markets, after which he would expect a double-digit decline in tech stocks.
